MN202611_gbp3q90ksf.t:
Korali Urumuri imaze imyaka isaga 20 mu murimo wo kwamamaza ubutumwa bwiza bwa Yesu Kristo binyuze mu ndirimbo, yashyize hanze indirimbo nshya yise ‘Bisunike’, iri mu zigize umuzingo wayo mushya w’indirimbo esheshatu witwa ‘Abirusha imbaraga’ .

Iyi ndirimbo yakozwe mu buryo bwa Live Recording, ikubiyemo ubutumwa bugaruka ku mbaraga z’Imana n’uburyo ishobora gufasha umuntu gutsinda ibimugoye, ikamusunikira imbere mu gihe yumva afite ibimuremereye nk’imisozi iri mu nzira ye.

Korali Urumuri ivuga ko ‘Bisunike’ ari indirimbo ishobora gukora ku mutima wa buri wese, yaba uwamaze kubona ibisubizo by’amasengesho ye cyangwa ugitegereje kubona imbaraga z’Imana mu buzima bwe.

Ni ubutumwa iyi korali yifuza kugeza ku bantu benshi, isaba Abanyarwanda muri rusange n’abakunzi bayo by’umwihariko kuyumva no kuyisangiza abandi kugira ngo ikomeze gukwirakwiza ubutumwa bwiza ku Isi hose.

‘Bisunike’ ni imwe mu ndirimbo esheshatu zigize umuzingo mushya Chorale Urumuri yakoze mu 2026, iwita ‘Abirusha imbaraga’.

Uyu muzingo wakozwe mu buryo bugezweho bwa Live Recording, mu rwego rwo gukomeza kugeza ku bakunzi b’iyi korali ibihangano bifite ubutumwa bwubaka imitima kandi bigaruka ku mbaraga z’Imana mu buzima bw’abantu.

Iyi ndirimbo kandi ntireba gusa abamaze kubona ibisubizo by’ibyo basabye Imana, ahubwo inareba abacyitegereje, ikabibutsa gukomeza kugira ukwizera no gutegereza imbaraga zayo.

Korali Urumuri yatangiye mu Mata 2002, ishingwa ku gitekerezo cy’abantu bane bakomokaga mu matorero atandukanye yo muri paruwasi imwe, bahurizaga ku cyifuzo cyo gukorera Imana binyuze mu ndirimbo.

Muri Kanama 2003, yatangiye kuririmba mu materaniro yo ku wa Gatanu, rimwe na rimwe igahabwa umwanya no mu materaniro yo ku Cyumweru.

Bitewe n’uko ibihangano byayo byakundwaga, muri Kanama 2004 hateranye inama yemeza ko iba korali yemewe, ishyirirwaho ubuyobozi. Icyo gihe yatangiye kuyoborwa na Ernestine Nyirabahizi.

Mu 2005 ni bwo yahawe izina rya Chorale Urumuri, ikomeza urugendo rwo kuririmba no kwamamaza ubutumwa bwiza bwa Yesu Kristo.

Mu rwego rwo gukomeza gukwirakwiza ubutumwa bwiza binyuze mu bihangano, Chorale Urumuri yakoze indirimbo umunani z’amashusho mu 2018, iza ziyongera ku ndirimbo eshanu z’amajwi yakoze mu 2020.

Ibi bikorwa byari bigamije kugeza Ijambo ry’Imana ku bantu benshi, kubaka imitima yabo no kubafasha gukomeza kugira icyizere.

Uretse ibijyanye n’umuziki, iyi korali yanagize uruhare mu bikorwa by’ubufasha, by’umwihariko ifasha bamwe mu Banyarwanda batishoboye kubona ubwisungane mu kwivuza ndetse n’ubundi bufasha bugamije kunoza imibereho yabo.

Kuri ubu, Chorale Urumuri iyobowe na Nsengiyumva Philemon, ikaba imaze kugira umuryango mugari w’abantu barenga 150.

Iyi korali ivuga ko intego yayo atari ukwamamaza ubutumwa bwiza gusa, ahubwo ari no gukomeza kugira uruhare mu iterambere ry’abayigize n’Abanyarwanda muri rusange, binyuze mu bikorwa by’urukundo, inama n’ubufasha butandukanye.

Nyuma y’imyaka isaga 20 itangijwe n’abantu bane, Chorale Urumuri ikomeje urugendo rwo kugeza ubutumwa bwiza bwa Kristo ku batuye Isi, ikoresheje indirimbo n’ibikorwa bigamije kubaka imibereho myiza y’abantu.

MN202611_oq9kkj0269.t:
Umuhanzikazi Nshuti Delice uzwi nka Santha mu muziki, yasobanuye impamvu yahisemo umukinnyi wa filime Ricky Ozil mu mashusho y’indirimbo ye nshya yise ‘Wazunga’, avuga ko ari umuntu ushoboye kugaragaza amarangamutima y’urukundo yashakaga kugeza ku bakunzi b’umuziki.

Santha yavuze ko igihe yatekerezaga kuri aya mashusho atashakaga gusa kubona amashusho meza, ahubwo yashakaga ko agira inkuru n’ubutumwa bukora ku mitima y’abayareba.

Yavuze ko Ricky Ozil ari we wabonyeho ubushobozi bwo kugeza ku bantu amarangamutima yifuzaga kugaragaza muri iyi ndirimbo.

Yagize ati: “Nashakaga umuntu ushobora gutuma abantu bareba amashusho bumva urukundo, n’imbaraga zo kwifuza kugumana n’uwo ukunda kandi Ozil ni umuhanga muri byo.”

Santha yavuze ko muri iyi ndirimbo yashakaga guha ijambo abantu bigeze gukunda by’ukuri, ku buryo bazumva ko amarangamutima banyuzemo asobanukiwe.

Ati: “Nkora iyi ndirimbo nifuzaga ko umuntu wese uzayumva yarigeze gukunda byimazeyo azamenya ko hari abandi basobanukiwe amarangamutima ye.”

Ku bijyanye n’inkomoko y’igitekerezo cyo gukora ‘Wazunga’, uyu muhanzikazi yavuze ko cyaturutse ku marangamutima y’urukundo nyarwo, cyane cyane ubushake bwo kugumana n’umuntu ukunda nubwo mwahura n’ibibazo bitandukanye.

Ati: “Igitekerezo cyo kwandika iyi ndirimbo cyavuye ku marangamutima y’urukundo nyarwo. Nashakaga kugaragaza uko umuntu ashobora gukunda undi byimazeyo, ku buryo nubwo mu rukundo habamo ibihe bigoye, umutima we uba utiteguye kumurekura.”

Nubwo muri ‘Wazunga’ hagaragaramo ubutumwa bwo kwitangira uwo ukunda, Santha anagaragaza ko urukundo rudakwiye kubura kubahana, ko kugumana bigomba kuba amahitamo y’impande zombi ndetse ko hari igihe kurekura biba ngombwa.

‘Wazunga’ ni indirimbo ya gatatu Santha ashyize hanze nyuma ya ‘Ishimwe’ na ‘Akanyamuneza’. Akomeje urugendo rwo kwagura ibikorwa bye bya muzika no kumenyekanisha izina rye mu bakunzi b’umuziki.

MN202611_1habhazyq9l.t:
Ubuyobozi bwa ADEPR bunenga abavuga ko iri torero rivanga imiyoborere y’idini n’ibikorwa bya Politiki,bukavuga ko buri mu murongo mwiza igihugu n’Imana ishaka.

Mu ntangiriro z’Ukwezi ku Ukwakira uyu mwaka Abashumba b’Itorero rya Pentekote mu Rwanda (ADEPR) bitabiriye Itorero ry’igihugu ryabereye mu Kigo cy’Ubutore cya Nkumba mu Karere ka Burera. Iri torero ryamaze iminsi itandatu, kuva ku wa 5 kugeza ku wa 10 Ukwakira, 2026.

Ni na ryo dini rya mbere rifashe abashumba bakajya mu itorero, aho bajya kwigishwa indangagaciro na za Kirazira z’umuco nyarwanda, amateka y’igihugu ndetse n’izindi gahunda zitandukanye zireba igihugu.

Ubwo bari muri iryo torero, umushumba Mukuru w’Itorero rya ADEPR, Pasiteri Ndayizeye Isaïe, yavuze ko iri torero ryateguwe kugira ngo abaryitabiriye basobanukirwe neza ibyasenye u Rwanda n’Abanyarwanda, bityo bibafashe gufata ingamba zo kurwubaka no kururinda.

Ati “Iri torero ryateguwe hagamijwe gufasha abashumba n’abo bayobora kumenya amateka y’igihugu, bakamenya ibyasenye igihugu n’Abanyarwanda ndetse bikabafasha gufata ingamba zo kurwubaka no kururinda kugira ngo dufatanye kubaka u Rwanda twifuza.”

Bamwe bashimye intambwe ADEPR yateye abandi bararinenga

Ubusanzwe itorero rya ADEPR rizwiho kugira amahame arimo n’abuza abayoboke baryo kwambara imyenda igaragaza imususire y’umubiri irimo amapantalo ku bagore n’abakobwa, amajipo cyangwa amakanzu magufi,gusuka imisatsi n’andi asunikira umukirisitu mu mahame ngengamyitwarire y’iri dini.

Gusa icyatangaje abantu, ni uburyo abashumba b’abagore b’iri torero bagaragaye bambaye ipantalo ubwo bari mu itorero ,bagashinja abashumba kuvanga idini na Poltiki.

Uwiyita Umwungeri kuri X yagize ati “A DEPR nayo yarinjiriwe? Ubwo se agakiza kavangwa na Politiki gute?”

Undi nawe wiyita Rwanda_Says ati “ Hehe, no kongera guteranya inama ngo bagiye guhana umukristo w’umugore wambaye ipantalo.”

Undi nawe ati “bagore ba ADEPR bamaze imyaka babuzwa ipantalo, none abashumba bagiye kwambara ipantalo za gisirikare? K o bigeze ku itorero ry’igihugu ipantalo iremewe, ariko mu rusengero itemewe.”

Gusa hari bamwe bagaragaje ko ADEPR iri mu nzira nziza zo kubaka igihugu kizira ivangura.

Umwe yagize ati “ N i byiza ADEPR yemeye ko bamwe mu bashumba bayo bagize uruhare muri Jenoside, none iri gukosora amateka.”

Undi ati”I dini no kubaka igihugu bishobora kujyana, si ngombwa ko bitandukana”

Umushumba Mukuru Wungirije wa ADEPR , Pasiteri Rutagarama Eugène, yabwiye UMUSEKE ko kuba abashumba ba ADEPR baragiye gutorezwa inkumba bidakwiye guca igikuba.

Ati “ Ni igipimo cyerekana ko akazi ka gihari. Kujya kwiga amateka y’igihugu cyacu,bihurira he na Politiki? Reka bibe Plitiki,Politiki ikubwira kubana neza n’uwo muturanye, Politki ikubwira gukundana,Politiki ikubwira gukorera ku muhigo,iyo Politiki ni mbi he ?

Akomeza ati “ Icyaha cyaba ari ikihe mu gihe ari iyo kubaka Itorero, Abanyarwanda,kubaka umubiri wange,kubaka igihugu .Twahavanye icyifuzo ngo ni gute umunyarwanda yaca aha?”

Ubwo yasozaga itorero ry,aba bashumba ba ADEPR,Minisitiri w’Ubumwe bw’Abanyarwanda n’inshingano mboneragihugu,Dr Bizimana Jean Damascène, yashimye uruhare ADEPR igira mu iterambere ry’igihugu binyuze mu bikorwa bitandukanye, birimo uburezi, ubuvuzi n’izindi gahunda zifasha imibereho myiza y’Abanyarwanda.

Yanashimye uburyo iri torero ryitwaye mu rugendo rwo kubaka ubumwe bw’Abanyarwanda, agaragaza ko ryafashe imyanzuro ikomeye yo kwemera amakosa yakozwe na bamwe mu bari abayobozi baryo no kuyakosora.

Ati “N i mwebwe tubona mufite urugendo mwakoze kurusha andi madini n’amatorero. Ibyo mwabikoze mu bintu bigaragara binyuze mu kwinenga, kwigaya, kwiyemeza, gukosora no gufata inzira ikwiriye. ”

Yakomeje ati “Ntabwo mwagiye mu murongo wo gutsimbarara ngo aba bantu bamwe na bamwe barabasebya, babeshyera itorero, bararyikoma, bararihimbira, barakabya nk’uko tubibona mu madini amwe na mwe .”

Dr Bizimana yavuze ko ADEPR yicaye ikisuzuma, ikemera ko mu mateka yayo habayemo abashumba bakoze Jenoside, maze ifata umwanzuro wo kubambura ubushumba n’izindi nshingano kubera uruhare bayigizemo.

Ngo abashumba bagiye mu itorero ” kwiga indangagaciro na za Kirazira” ?? Amadini aragwira.Niba se batazi “Kirazira”,ni gute bakigisha indanga-gaciro za Gikristu?? Amahame dusanga muli bible,niyo yigisha abakristu “Kirazira” ituruka ku Mana (God’s Principles).Niyo Kirazira irenze izindi zose.Kirazira y’abantu,usanga ivangamo politike.Ndetse rimwe na rimwe ikigisha ibyo Imana itubuza.Urugero,iy’abantu yigisha kurwana,ndetse byaba ngombwa ukica.Kirazira y’Imana ikatubuza Kwica no Kurwana,ahubwo ikadusaba Gukunda abanzi bacu nkuko Matayo 26:52 havuga.Ikavuga ko Imana yanga umuntu wese umena amaraso y’undi nkuko Zabuli 5:6 havuga.

Based on the past six matches, Chris Davies' Birmingham City are first and Sheffield United fifth in the Championship form table

With League One and League Two clubs involved in the FA Cup this weekend, the Championship has a free run of the EFL.

So far England's second tier has served up its usual helping of drama and chaos in equal measure while sacking season seems to be in full swing.

Struggling Derby County open proceedings on Friday against Bolton Wanderers and we have picked out five things you may want to keep an eye out for on Saturday.

Birmingham City are unbeaten at home in the Championship this season

Tom Wagner and his Knighthead Capital Management hardly made an auspicious start as owners of Birmingham City.

Sacking boss John Eustace when they were sixth in the Championship and appointing Wayne Rooney took many by surprise and, with the former Manchester United and England striker winning only two of his 15 league games in charge before being replaced by Gary Rowett, relegation became a near certainty.

A rebuild under Chris Davies saw Blues pay a League One record fee to sign Jay Stansfield, with his 19 goals helping to fire them to a record-breaking promotion.

Last season brought consolidation and a 10th-place finish with the hope for a promotion tilt this time around and the early signs are promising.

A run of five wins from their past six games has propelled Davies' side up to third, and a chance to possibly go top by beating Swansea on Saturday (15:00 GMT).

"The league table is temporary at the moment and when I came in two-and-a-half years ago we'd just been relegated, so we've come a long way and we feel like we deserve to be where we are," said Davies after Tuesday's 3-0 win over Millwall.

Swansea's visit not only provides a good test for Birmingham's credentials but also of the Welshmen's powers of recovery.

A 4-0 thrashing of Blackburn last weekend was sandwiched in between a 5-0 walloping by QPR and Tuesday's 3-1 reverse at Portsmouth which has seen Vitor Matos' side fall out of the automatic promotion places.

This then feels like a first real test for both teams to prove their worth.

Scott Parker made 129 appearances during four years as a West Ham player

A week is a long time in football, just ask West Ham United fans.

From the boos and jeers following a home defeat by West Brom last Saturday came the sacking of boss Nuno Espirito Santo, the appointment of Scott Parker and a crazy 3-3 draw at Cardiff City - such is the life of a Hammers supporter.

Parker is back at the club he served for four years as a player, bringing with him a reputation as a man who knows how to get teams out of the Championship. The 46-year-old has already won promotion with Fulham, Bournemouth and Burnley.

"I've been in this division three times and I've got out of this division three times. This is a tough division, there is absolutely no denying it," Parker said.

"I will use every ounce of my experience, every ounce of my knowledge, to have an understanding of what we're going to need to bring consistency."

The first 45 minutes of his tenure was a perfect example of the task facing him as the Hammers went 3-0 down at Cardiff before fighting back to claim an unlikely point.

Saturday's trip to Blackburn (15:00 GMT) brings them up against a side who have lost two on the bounce but have a habit of producing a result just when you think they are on the slide.

Nathan Jones' Charlton have not won since the end of August

Now, unless you are a Sheffield United supporter you may not have noticed them so far this season but there they are, quietly going about their business in ninth place.

With four wins from their past six games the Blades have tip-toed their way into the play-off frame and only five points short of the top two.

"I'm not getting carried away, we needed to get to the first international break and work a few things out which we've done - I want to build something here and some stuff works and some doesn't so we're learning on the job," head coach Chris Wilder said after Tuesday's Sydie Peck - inspired win at Preston.

Contrast Sheffield United's emotions with those of Charlton for whom second-season syndrome is snapping at their heels.

From the highs of being top of the table after three successive wins to start the season, the Addicks have plunged to four straight defeats with no victory since the end of August.

Suddenly Saturday's meeting at The Valley (15:00 GMT) has a lot riding on it for both teams.

Preston have won just one league game this season

When Graham Alexander returned to the scene of past glories as a player to become Preston North End manager towards the end of September his new team were second from bottom, three points short of the safety line.

Six games into his tenure they are now nine points adrift with a solitary draw to show for their efforts. If he had any doubt as to the size of the job he had taken on, the half-a-dozen matches since will have opened his eyes fully.

"I wanted it to be a fresh start when I came in but they're carrying baggage of the past and I can understand that, and it's my job and the coaching staff to get them to put that down and see the rest of the season as an opportunity," Alexander told BBC Radio Lancashire.

If you were looking for a team who might be carrying baggage then Southampton would have been one given the fallout from Spygate, but Saints' season has been sailing along.

Their two hiccups have come away from home, but having taken seven points from their past nine on the road they will surely be feeling confident before their trip to Deepdale (15:00 GMT).

Preston North End manager Graham Alexander

James Morrison spent 12 years at West Brom as a player

Throughout a rather tempestuous 2025-26 season, the one constant at West Bromwich Albion was James Morrison.

Having worked their way through Ryan Mason and Eric Ramsay, Morrison was called upon to take the reins before being handed the role permanently in April as reward for steering them clear of relegation.

A five-game unbeaten run, including impressive wins over Wrexham, Blackburn and West Ham has pushed Albion into the top six going into Saturday's meeting with Millwall at The Hawthorns (15:00 GMT).

A lengthy injury list has so far prevented the Londoners from replicating last season's form which took them to the brink of automatic promotion before play-off heartbreak.

These two are seeking to be contenders for at least a top-eight finish and a result for either may show us who is the real deal and who might just be a pretender.

BBC Sport will have live text coverage of all the weekend's Championship action starting on Friday with Derby County v Bolton Wanderers (20:00 GMT).

MN202611_ljkqcogwli.t:
Major tech firms have seen their stock values fall after a sell-off by investors following the US midterm elections.

The fall in the value of their shares across the world has been blamed on an expectation of a slowdown in AI development, although it comes after sharp rises over recent years.

As companies grow, they may issue shares. Many of the largest companies in the UK have shares which are bought and sold on the London Stock Exchange.

Their collective performance is often quoted amid a blizzard of numbers that may feel confusing and irrelevant.

Booms or falls in the stock market make the news, but rarely does anyone mention the FTSE 100 during a coffee with friends.

Yet, there are good reasons why this performance affects your life and finances.

Many people's initial reaction to "the markets" is that they are not directly affected, because they do not invest money.

Yet there are millions of people with a pension - either private or through work - who will see their savings (in what is known as a defined contribution pension) invested by pension schemes. The value of their savings pot is influenced by the performance of these investments.

Pension savers mostly let experts choose where to invest this money to help it grow. Widespread falls in share prices are likely to be bad news for pension savers.

Hundreds of billions of pounds are held in defined contribution pensions at the moment.

So big rises or falls can affect your pension, but the advice is to remember that pension savings, like any investments, are usually a long-term bet.

Experts say that investors have always had to ride economic shocks. Investments, by definition, require a long-term outlook and strategy. So, they are urging people not to panic in such circumstances or make knee-jerk decisions.

Some people have a pension which promises a specific value, depending on their salary. Others have no pension at all.

Millions of people have been automatically enrolled into a pension and may have not really noticed. Those schemes see employers divert wages into a pension and contribute some money themselves. The government adds a little in tax relief.

In every case, the value of these pension savings is affected by investment performance. So "the markets" matter - maybe not as much as everyday wages, but for future pensions.

Timing is more critical for those at retirement age, as this may be when a retiree uses their pension pot to buy a retirement income, or annuity. The bigger the pot, the more income they will get in retirement.

As you approach retirement age, pension pots tend to be moved to less risky investments, such as government bonds. When stock markets fall, these bonds can do better.

Anyone who has a pension pot invested and is taking an income from it will again see their investment go up and down with the stock markets.

That could mean getting less than you expected if you cash in too much after stock markets have fallen, making it important to plan how to make up any of this shortfall, experts say.

However, higher interest rates tend to mean better rates offered on annuities, and there is a chance of more rate rises in the UK by the Bank of England.

If share prices fall for an extended period then that could have an effect on jobs.

That's because investors in the company expect a return on that investment.

When it falls for a while, then they would expect the business to address issues, for example by cutting costs, and therefore jobs.

There is a huge element of the unknown here though. Companies have to consider lots of factors when making decisions on investment and employment.

In purely investment terms, lower share prices can offer an opportunity to buy, in the hope that over the long term, they recover and rise. Many people will do this initially through a stocks and shares Individual Savings Account (Isa).

However, it is worth noting that the sell-off in tech stocks in particular came after big rises, so long-term investors are still likely to have seen gains.

Experts and regulators are at pains to point out that investments can go down as well as up, and urge people not to put everything into one investment, but to diversify.

Some people invest money in what are known as tracker funds. These go up and down in line with the performance of a certain index, such as the FTSE 100.

So if the index falls, so does the value of their investments and vice versa. One advantage of these funds is that they often cost relatively little to sign up to.

Yes, and millions of people do, but experts stress that a long-term strategy is required to ride out short-term falls. It is also important to ensure cash savings are held too, so unexpected expenses - like the need for a replacement boiler - can be covered.

The government is keen to get people in the UK to invest more, partly because it says that will help UK economic growth and partly because it is much more popular among individuals in the US and some parts of Europe.

It backed an advertising campaign to encourage people to invest, funded by some of the UK's biggest financial services firms.

But the choice of "Savvy the Squirrel" to front the campaign has raised some eyebrows. Some question whether the push could get anywhere close to the success of the Tell Sid adverts of the 1980s, which encouraged people to invest in the newly privatised British Gas.

When we see big shifts in the stock markets there can also be fluctuations in the value of currencies and exchange rates.

As a result, prices could go up, but could also go down.

Upheaval to economies across the world, to oil prices and so on, have a big impact on what we pay at home for goods and services, so there are lots of factors in play.

*Ku bitaro by’i Rilima basabye kwishyura Frw 800,000 ntayo afite, yiringiye abagiraneza *Uyu mubyeyi aboneka kuri nomero 0796680252 cyangwa 0790107700

Uwera Agnes wo mu Karere ka Kamonyi mu Murenge wa Runda, Akagari ka Gihara, Umudugudu wa Nyagitare, arasaba abagiraneza kumufasha kuvuza umwana we witwa Ngenzi Edwin ufite uburwayi bukomatanyije.

Uyu mubyeyi avuga ko umwana we w’imyaka irindwi yafashwe n’uburwayi bwo guhinamirana ingingo akivuka bitewe n’uko yavutse ananiwe.

Yongeraho ko abaganga bamubwiye ko umwana we afite ubwonko bwangiritse.

Uwera Agnes yabwiye UMUSEKE ko yagerageje kuvuza uyu mwana ku Bitaro byita ku barwayi bo mu mutwe i Ndera ariko imiti bamuhaga ntigire icyo itanga.

Ati “Bamaze kumunyuza mu cyuma bambwiye ko afite ikibazo cy’ubwonko businziriye, bambwira ko ngomba kubukangura. Bampa imiti izajya ibukangura.

Imiti najyaga kuyifata i Ndera ariko iyo miti ikamwangiza. Narayimuhaga agahwera, ntiyongere kweguka kandi mu buzima busanzwe yabaga yegutse, ari nko kureba nk’imbere.

Akajya ahora asinziriye ntarye, ntanywe, nabaza muganga ko imiti iri kumwangiza, akambwira ngo bamuhaye imiti ihura n’indwara ye.”

Uyu mubyeyi avuga ko yafashe icyemezo cyo kujya kumuvuriza mu Bitaro bivura indwara z’amagufwa by’i Rilima mu Karere ka Bugesera, ariko bamusaba kugira amafaranga atanga angana hafi n’ibihumbi 800Frw ariko agorwa no kuba nta bushobozi, bityo agasaba abagiraneza kumufasha.

Ati “Bampaye bafigitire ngo avurwe. Iyo fagitire nayitanze ku Murenge, Umurenge uyijyana ku Karere. Ibyo byose narabikoze mu kwezi kwa 12 umwaka ushize.

Nkajya nkomeza kubaza amakuru, bakambwira ko bazampamagara ariko na n’ubu nta muntu urampamagara. Bari bananyemereye n’akagare kajya kamufasha ariko kugeza ubu na ko sindakabona.”

Umunyamabanga Nshingwabikorwa w’Umurenge wa Runda, Jean Pierre Egide Ndayisaba yabwiye UMUSEKE ko uyu muturage yakongera akegera ubuyobozi bukamufasha kuvuza umwana we.

Ati “Aze ku Murenge, ubwo bufasha turabugira. Aze tumufasha ajyane umwana we kwa Muganga.”

Uyu mubyeyi avuga ko aramutse abonye abagiraneza bamufasha kuvuza umwana we, yavurwa agakira ikibazo cy’ingingo n’ibibazo by’ubwonko bwasinziriye bwakongera bugakanguka.

MN202611_tp52lg1poi.t:
Across the continent, xenophobic attacks have exposed the hostility directed at fellow Africans.

America’s evolving political representation raises an uncomfortable question for Africa: Can we genuinely embrace democracy while allowing ancestry, ethnicity and perceived foreignness to determine who belongs and who has the right to lead?

The recently concluded United States midterm elections offer an interesting opportunity for reflection, particularly for those of us observing political developments from Africa. Beyond the victories and defeats of political parties, these elections bring into focus a deeper question about citizenship, identity, representation and the meaning of belonging in a democratic society.

Consider the changing face of political representation in America. These elections produced several historic breakthroughs that challenge long-held assumptions about who can occupy positions of political authority. Georgia elected Keisha Lance Bottoms as the first Black woman governor in American history.

New Mexico elected Deb Haaland, making her the first Native American woman to become a governor. Texas elected Gina Hinojosa as its first Latina governor, while Minnesota elected Peggy Flanagan as the first Native American woman to serve in the US Senate.

In New Hampshire, Chris Pappas became the first openly gay man elected to the US Senate. Wisconsin also elected David Crowley as its first Black governor.

These achievements are significant not simply because they represent historical firsts, but because they challenge established assumptions about who can govern, who can represent a nation and whose voice deserves a place in political leadership.

America is certainly not a model of perfect equality. Its history is marked by slavery, segregation, racial violence and persistent discrimination.

Yet its democratic journey presents Africa with an important question: Why should a person’s ancestry remain a political liability in a country where that person is a legitimate citizen?

There is perhaps an even deeper lesson here. Political leaders do not simply find their way into office; they must earn the support of voters. Citizens, through their ballots, can choose candidates whose racial backgrounds, ancestry, gender or identities differ from their own.

Equally important, constitutional and democratic institutions establish rules that protect the electoral process. An incumbent president cannot simply overturn a legitimate election because they dislike the identity or background of the person voters have chosen.

This presents an interesting question for Africa.

Are our societies equally prepared to elect people they perceive as descendants of foreigners, even when those individuals are citizens and meet the constitutional requirements for leadership? Do our institutions adequately protect their right to compete for political office? Or have ideas about indigenous identity, ancestral ownership and national belonging become so deeply rooted that even constitutional guarantees struggle to overcome them?

The contradiction deserves serious examination. In some African societies, sections of the electorate may be willing to look beyond ethnic and ancestral boundaries.

Yet political rhetoric and identity-based mobilisation can create barriers around who is considered entitled to lead. In other cases, exclusionary attitudes may also exist among voters themselves. The challenge, therefore, is not only institutional but also political and social.

Across the continent, xenophobic attacks have exposed the hostility directed at fellow Africans, particularly migrants from countries such as Zimbabwe, Mozambique and Nigeria in South Africa. People who establish businesses, create employment and contribute to local economies can become targets simply because they are perceived as foreigners.

Beyond xenophobia, questions of indigenous citizenship, ancestral origins and parental nationality have also become controversial features of constitutional and political debates. Zambia, for instance, has experienced prolonged controversy surrounding presidential eligibility requirements, particularly constitutional provisions relating to the citizenship of a candidate’s parents.

Of course, countries have legitimate reasons to establish citizenship requirements for public office. National sovereignty, constitutional order and security are important considerations that cannot simply be dismissed. However, there is a fundamental difference between establishing legitimate eligibility requirements and creating barriers that deliberately exclude individuals because of their ancestry or perceived origins.

Consider the contradiction: someone may be born in an African country, educated there, speak its languages, pay taxes, employ its citizens and invest their entire life in its development, yet still face questions about whether they genuinely belong.

Meanwhile, another person may enjoy unquestioned acceptance simply because their ancestors have deeper historical connections to that territory.

Is ancestral proximity really a more reliable measure of national commitment than a person’s actual contribution to society?

Africa must also confront the historical irony surrounding its geographical boundaries. Many of our present borders emerged from colonial arrangements that divided communities, combined territories and disregarded existing cultural relationships. As a result, African families have cross-border roots, share languages, intermarry and maintain historical connections that existed long before modern nation-states were established.

It is therefore contradictory that we celebrate Pan-Africanism, promote continental integration, establish the African Continental Free Trade Area and advocate greater regional mobility while sometimes treating fellow Africans as strangers simply because colonial geography placed them on opposite sides of a border.

We cannot convincingly advocate African unity while practising exclusion within our own societies.

More importantly, political representation should not become another instrument of exclusion. Historical marginalisation deserves recognition, and inclusive political participation is essential. However, inclusion should expand opportunities rather than create new categories of people considered unsuitable for leadership.

The standard should be straightforward: citizenship establishes legitimate belonging, constitutional rights protect political participation, and voters determine whom they wish to entrust with leadership, within the requirements of the law.

A person’s surname, accent, complexion or grandparents’ birthplace should not automatically become a referendum on their loyalty to the country.

The American experience does not offer a perfect democratic model, and greater political representation does not automatically translate into competent governance. Elected leaders must still demonstrate integrity, accountability and the ability to deliver. Nevertheless, the expansion of political representation provides an important opportunity for African societies to reconsider their own assumptions about identity, citizenship and leadership.

Our greatest resource is not ancestral purity. It is human potential.

Perhaps the real question is not where someone’s grandparents came from, but what that person is prepared to contribute to the country.

A nation should not be an inheritance reserved for families with the oldest roots. It should be a shared responsibility entrusted to capable and accountable citizens.

The author, Sylivanus M. Karemera is Station Manager, KT Radio 96.7FM, which is under Kigali Today Ltd

MN202611_1rkz2yprdr3.t:
Rwanda deserves recognition for Miss Baza, an innovative voice-first artificial intelligence assistant launched by MTN Rwanda in partnership with Viamo. It brings AI closer to ordinary citizens, including those without smartphones, mobile internet or mobile applications.

By dialling 845 from an MTN line, users can ask questions and receive spoken responses. The service supports Kinyarwanda, English, French and Kiswahili, covering areas such as healthcare, agriculture, financial literacy, land titles and local government services. Users receive 30 free minutes monthly, after which calls cost RWF 45 per minute.

This is a commendable innovation. It recognizes that access to technology should not be determined by smartphone ownership. However, beyond the impressive experience, there is a bigger technological story worth examining.

What exactly powers Miss Baza, and where does Rwanda stand in owning that technology?

When someone calls Miss Baza, several systems work together. MTN provides the telecommunications network and access through short-code 845. Viamo provides the voice platform and interactive voice response infrastructure. Pindo, working with Viamo, contributes to Kinyarwanda speech processing. Google’s Gemini provides the underlying generative AI capabilities, while local information sources, including Eden Care, contribute contextual knowledge relevant to Rwandan services.

The spoken question is converted into information the AI can process. The model generates a response, which is subsequently converted into speech and delivered to the caller. This collaboration brings together local and international capabilities. But contributing to a product is not necessarily the same as owning its underlying technology.

Google developed Gemini, the foundational AI model powering the service. Viamo contributes its voice platform and orchestration technology. MTN Rwanda provides the telecommunications infrastructure, distribution and customer access. Pindo contributes local language-processing capabilities.

These are valuable contributions, but they raise important questions about intellectual property.

Does MTN Rwanda own the complete source code? Who owns improvements made to the system? Who controls the language resources developed through the collaboration? Can Rwandan engineers independently modify and reproduce the entire architecture?

The specific contractual arrangements governing Miss Baza’s intellectual property have not been publicly established. Nevertheless, owning a service or its brand does not automatically mean owning the technology behind it.

Every conversation with Miss Baza potentially generates valuable information about citizens, their languages, questions, needs and interactions.

Where are voice recordings and transcripts processed and stored? Who can access them? How long are they retained? Are conversations used to improve AI systems? Under what agreements? We should not assume that Google trains its models on these conversations. That requires evidence. But the processing arrangements, data-retention policies and responsibilities of each partner deserve transparency.

There is also an economic question: if local language resources and conversational data contribute to improving AI systems, who ultimately captures the resulting value?

There are clear advantages to this arrangement. MTN can launch quickly without building a foundational AI model or investing immediately in expensive GPU infrastructure. It benefits from Google’s established AI capabilities and Viamo’s voice technology. Citizens gain access to services through ordinary telephones.

However, dependence carries risks. Changes in API pricing, licensing conditions or international service availability could affect operations. Local engineers can maintain components they control, but they cannot independently repair Google’s proprietary model or Viamo’s closed systems without the necessary access and rights.

This is not an argument against international partnerships. It is an argument for ensuring that partnerships build local technical capacity rather than permanent dependence.

Africa has historically exported raw materials and imported finished products. We must ask whether a similar pattern is emerging in artificial intelligence.

Our languages, accents, cultural knowledge and human interactions are valuable resources. They can contribute to AI development. Yet if foundational models, computing infrastructure and intellectual property remain externally controlled, Africa risks becoming a market and source of inputs for technologies whose highest-value assets are owned elsewhere.

Miss Baza is an important achievement, and MTN Rwanda deserves recognition for making AI accessible through ordinary telephone calls.

But technological progress should not be measured only by how many citizens can use artificial intelligence. It should also be measured by how many local engineers can build it, how many companies own its intellectual property, and whether the country can operate and maintain the underlying architecture independently.

James Kaliisa is Co Founder & CTO of Nexus Inc., a Rwandan deep tech company building sovereign artificial intelligence infrastructure and digital systems for Africa.

James Kaliisa is a lawyer-turned-tech entrepreneur, software developer, and Co-Founder & CEO of Nexus Inc., a Rwandan deep-tech company building AI-powered infrastructure solutions for industries across multiple sectors.

MN202611_1bsxirxbq7f.t:
BK CEO Dr Diane Karusisi (2nd Left), entrepreneur Sina Gerard and Northern Province Governor Maurice Mugabowagahunde, together with other leaders as they prepared for meeting with businesspeople affected by the GOICO Plaza fire last month

MUSANZE – Bank of Kigali has pledged to continue supporting businesses and investors affected by the fire that destroyed GOICO Market in Musanze District, including through discussions on outstanding loans as they work to rebuild their businesses.

The commitment came during a client engagement tour in Musanze on Thursday, November 5, led by BK Chief Executive Officer Dr. Diane Karusisi and senior bank executives.

The visit was part of activities marking the bank’s 60th anniversary and was aimed at strengthening relationships with customers, understanding their businesses and projects, and identifying ways BK can support their growth.

The tour covered education institutions, an industrial company, as well as investors and traders affected by the GOICO Market fire.

The BK team began the day at Virunga Valley Academy, a school providing education from nursery through secondary level.

The discussions focused on the school’s activities and operations, as well as its partnership with BK. The bank thanked the school for its continued trust and said it would continue visiting other customers in Musanze to engage with them and understand their needs.

The team later visited INES-Ruhengeri, a higher learning institution focused on applied sciences, research and innovation.

Discussions at INES focused on the institution’s ongoing and planned projects and ways of strengthening its partnership with BK.

Karusisi said BK was proud of the institution’s contribution to Rwanda’s development and also praised INES graduates working at Bank of Kigali.

“We are proud of the contribution of INES Ruhengeri to the development of our country,” she said.

The INES leadership also presented projects for which it is seeking support, including a building currently under construction, student workshops and a Digital Hub.

The institution also plans to establish a clinic that would provide health services to people living around the school while giving students studying health-related programmes a place to gain practical experience.

BK officials toured more than 26 laboratories at the institution and discussed plans to further expand its capacity.

Fr. Dr. Jean Bosco Baribeshya, head of INES-Ruhengeri, praised the partnership with BK, saying the bank had supported the institution through different forms of financing, including loans used to expand its operations.

“We are pleased to receive BK today. It is a bank that wants the development of this country, and that is also what we are pursuing in education,” he said.

“Of course, it is where we channel the money we use, but it also helps us by providing loans when we want to expand our activities, which enables us to make further progress.”

He said INES wanted to continue working with BK on its planned projects.

The BK team also visited Excel International Academy, where discussions similarly focused on the institution’s activities, its relationship with the bank and areas where further support could be provided.

The tour also included A1 Iron & Steel Rwanda, where BK engaged with the company about its operations and investment plans.

The most pressing discussions came when Karusisi met investors who participated in the construction of GOICO Market and traders who operated there.

The market was destroyed by fire, leaving businesses facing losses while some investors and traders still have outstanding loans.

The affected business owners explained the impact of the fire and the assistance they need to rebuild.

Tugengwenayo Theonase, Chairperson of the Private Sector Federation in the Northern Province, said BK had been involved in financing GOICO from the beginning and had continued supporting the investors when they encountered difficulties.

“In that investment project to build GOICO Market, which was later destroyed by fire, BK gave us a loan at the beginning of the construction, and even when we encountered challenges along the way, it continued to support us,” he said.

Tugengwenayo said loans amounting to nearly Rwf1 billion remained unpaid following the fire.

He asked BK to consider easing repayment conditions for the affected investors, including suspending interest payments while they deal with the consequences of the disaster.

The fire has therefore left investors facing two challenges: rebuilding businesses and meeting financial obligations linked to businesses that were destroyed or severely affected.

Northern Province Governor Mugabowagahunde Maurice thanked BK for continuing to engage people affected by the GOICO fire.

He said the discussions were intended to find practical solutions that would enable traders and investors to resume their activities.

“We wanted to meet with BK today, together with those who built GOICO and those who operated in this market, following the disaster that affected our market,” he said.

“Some of those who operated in this market had loans from BK, and the building itself had also been constructed with a BK loan that had not yet been fully repaid.”

Mugabowagahunde said the province wanted to work with BK on ways of easing loan repayments for traders and owners of the market, while also helping other affected businesses obtain support to recover.

“We agreed that those who worked in this market and had loans, as well as others who need loans, should have an opportunity to discuss their challenges with the bank,” he said.

“The next step is to establish a mechanism at the BK branch so that everyone can go there, have their individual situation assessed and receive support from there.”

The governor also said the province wants other investment projects in Musanze to continue rather than being halted because of the difficulties faced by individual businesses.

He said continued investment would be important to maintaining economic growth in the district.

Mugabowagahunde also praised BK’s approach of visiting customers and listening to their concerns, and encouraged other banks to adopt a similar approach.

Karusisi said the Musanze visit was designed to go beyond routine banking services by allowing the bank’s senior management to meet customers directly and understand the challenges they face.

“Today we came to Musanze, where many of our customers suffered losses, including those who built GOICO and those who operated there, so that we can discuss and develop strategies to rebuild, but also to revive businesses in Musanze more broadly,” she said.

Dr Karusisi said the people visited during the tour were BK customers whose businesses and projects the bank wanted to understand better.

“We thank them for working with us and entrusting their businesses to us. We also want to understand their ambitions and strategies so that we can help them implement them,” Karusisi said.

“A bank’s job is to support businesses so that their owners can achieve their dreams.”

She said supporting businesses and investment was part of BK’s wider contribution to Rwanda’s economy through job creation, increased production and tax revenues.

On INES-Ruhengeri, Karusisi said the institution had presented several projects that could contribute to improving the quality of education.

“INES Ruhengeri is a major institution that we have worked with for a long time. They showed us their plans, the buildings they have, where they want to build a Digital Hub and where they want to build student workshops to improve the quality of education,” she said.

“They showed us how far they have come and where they would like BK to support them so that they can complete those buildings.”

She said BK would continue discussing the institution’s needs and potential areas of support.

The Musanze tour formed part of BK’s activities marking its 60th anniversary.

Unlike the bank’s earlier BK@60 public celebrations, including football and music events in Rubavu, the November 5 programme focused primarily on direct engagement with customers.

BK shared footage of the visits to Virunga Valley Academy and INES-Ruhengeri through its official social media channels under the bank’s BK60 campaign.

The bank said the customer outreach is intended to strengthen its relationship with clients, understand their projects and challenges, and identify opportunities for further collaboration.

The Musanze visit also comes as BK seeks to position itself as a long-term financial partner to businesses and institutions across the country.

Karusisi said that after more than six decades of operations in Rwanda, the bank would continue reaching out to customers, listening to their needs and working with them to implement their projects.

For the businesses affected by the GOICO fire, that engagement now includes finding ways to manage outstanding financial obligations while creating conditions for them to rebuild.

The discussions between BK, the provincial authorities, investors and traders are expected to provide a basis for affected customers to present their individual cases at the BK Musanze branch and explore possible solutions.

MN202611_123gaea96v4.t:
President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud's four-year mandate expired in May

Somalia's Supreme Court has ruled that President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud unlawfully extended his term, escalating a political crisis and a standoff between the presidency and judiciary.

Thursday's ruling came a day after Mohamud dismissed Chief Justice Bashe Yusuf Ahmed - a move which the court said the president lacked the authority to take.

The court also ordered political leaders to agree on an electoral plan within 30 days and hold elections within 90 days, potentially disrupting government plans for nationwide polls next year.

Mohamud's four-year mandate expired in May, but his administration extended it by a year through law changes approved by parliament in March.

Opposition groups accuse him of using the constitutional changes to prolong his rule.

But the president insists the reforms are necessary to move Somalia towards fully democratic elections, replacing the clan-based system in which elders pick their representatives which has been used since 2012.

Somalia last held nationwide direct elections in 1969 and has been wracked by civil war for more than 30 years, with Islamist militant group al-Shabab controlling many rural areas.

Somalia's president: They tried to kill me five times

On Thursday, the Supreme Court ruled that the constitutional changes could not be applied retrospectively to the president's current term.

In a separate decision, the court declared the chief justice's dismissal "null and void", accusing the presidency of interfering with judicial independence.

The president appointed Ibrahim Idle Suleiman, who previously held the position, to replace Ahmed.

The presidency said the dismissal followed complaints about the administration of justice and was intended to achieve a just and transparent judiciary.

But the court rejected that explanation, insisting that the chief justice could only be removed through established constitutional procedures.

Former President Sharif Sheikh Ahmed welcomed the court ruling, saying "the country is facing a grave political crisis", calling on Mohamud to embrace a consensus-based approach.

The confrontation escalated on Thursday when former Prime Minister Hassan Ali Khaire accused the president of deploying security forces to the Supreme Court and attempting to arrest its chief justice.

Khaire accused the president of launching an "assault on the Supreme Court", according to the AFP news agency.

"Somalia stands at a dangerous juncture. The dismantling of our judiciary is a direct threat to the rule of law," he said.

AFP said it could not independently verify the reported security deployment, although photographs circulating in Somali media appeared to show armed personnel inside the court compound.

The rulings have thrown Somalia's electoral timetable into uncertainty.

The electoral commission has scheduled parliamentary elections for 15 April 2027 and a presidential vote a month later, but opposition groups and the regional administrations of Puntland and Jubaland reject the timetable.

Mohamud has called for national talks from 14 to 18 November to resolve the deadlock, but opposition leaders have questioned his legitimacy to convene the discussions.

The political turmoil comes as Somalia continues to battle al-Shabab, which controls large parts of the countryside despite years of military operations.

Uganda, the largest contributor of troops to the African Union mission fighting the militants, announced this week that it planned to withdraw its forces by the end of the year , adding to concerns about Somalia's security.

Iran appears to be undertaking significant new construction near at least two of its major missile sites and repairing bases damaged by months of US and Israeli air strikes, analysis of satellite images suggests.

Evidence of digging and new buildings are visible in satellite imagery taken in November at the Garmdareh military base in Karaj near the capital Tehran and the Shahroud base in the north, analysts at British intelligence company MAIAR, who reviewed the photos, told BBC Verify.

At least 12 other military sites, including missile complexes and air bases, appear to show signs of repairs. New roofs have been built on destroyed buildings at the Kermanshah missile base in western Iran, near the border with Iraq, while damaged buildings and debris have been cleared at the Parchin military complex - which has been repeatedly repaired despite a succession of air strikes - east of the capital.

The excavations near Shahroud could potentially be related to the production of missiles, said Jim Lamson, a former CIA analyst who focused on Iran. He said that because the nearby air base at Shahroud has been targeted multiple times in recent years, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) is probably trying to find ways to move its production facilities underground.

A MAIAR analyst said that Iran has "a pattern of moving infrastructure underground to protect them from further strikes". Mark Mellett, a defence analyst and former head of the Irish military, said the construction of underground facilities had the added benefit of making it "harder for outside observers to assess the extent and operational status".

Speculation has mounted in recent weeks that the US could resume attacks on Iran after the midterm elections held earlier this week. But on Wednesday Vice-President JD Vance cited the war's unpopularity with voters for the Republicans' poor performance in this week's poll, saying that it may have cost his party control of the Senate "for the next 6 years".

At multiple bases across the country, Iranian forces have focused on carrying-out small-scale repairs to complexes which have been heavily damaged by air strikes since the start of the US-Israeli war.

Analysts said that satellite images appear to show that significant construction has been completed at the Taleghan 2 facility at the Parchin military complex, with damaged buildings levelled and the aftermath of attacks on an underground bunker repaired and reinforced with concrete.

At Karaj , external and Shahroud, satellite images appear to show significant excavation. At Karaj, multiple vehicles were visible in satellite images, while improvements appear to have been carried out to the nearby airbase.

The images from Karaj appear to show "a new portal for an underground facility", said Sam Lair, research analyst at the Foreign Policy Research Institute (FPRI), which has looked extensively into recent developments at Iranian sites.

Analysis from Janes also indicates there appears to be a new facility under construction at Karaj, including tunnel entrances and structures which could indicate an expansion of nearby damaged or destroyed missile bases - or could also be for storage or other purposes.

The construction work is unlikely to be part of an effort to deceive foreign intelligence agencies, said Janes analyst Sean O'Connor. He said such a project "would be costly and may achieve little".

The developments come after repeated assurances from the White House that US-Israeli attacks have depleted the Iranian armed forces, which US President Donald Trump dismissed as a "complete and total mess".

A Pentagon spokesperson previously said that the US had "destroyed up to 90% of Iran's drone, ballistic missile, and naval industrial base" and "significantly degraded" the country's ability to launch drone and missile attacks.

But Iran claims it retains large stockpiles of missiles, and footage broadcast on state TV this week claimed to show dozens of missiles at the entrance to an underground facility in southern Iran. Back in August, state TV footage also claimed to show Khordad surface-to-air missiles emerging out of a tunnel near the southern city of Bandar Abbas , external .

A MAIAR analyst also identified new construction and excavations outside tunnel entrances near the city of Qom, close to the Fordo underground uranium enrichment complex, which has been bombed by both the US and Israel multiple times.

Activity related to military assets would show that Tehran is bracing itself for further attacks by the US and Israel, said Mark Cancian, a military analyst with International Security Program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS).

"The purpose is to better defend itself against future attacks," he said. "It also indicates a priority on rebuilding military capability rather than rehabilitating the economy."

Additional reporting by Barbara Metzler.

MN202611_did0q5903v.t:
The November international break is almost upon us, which always means one thing - the managerial merry-go-round is about to properly get into gear.

It's known as 'sacking season' for a reason - the new campaign has started to take shape and I know from experience that any manager who is not winning games will always be sleeping with just one eye closed, and the other one open.

At any club on a poor run of results, the owners and supporters will be questioning whether the manager is the right fit to continue.

This two-week break from domestic games is the ideal opportunity to blood the new incumbent and give them a period of getting to know everyone before the games start up again.

That means it is 'hiring season' too, but there are always far more out-of-work managers than vacant positions.

Since the start of last season, 60 different managers have resigned or been sacked by teams in the Premier League and Football League. Three of them left to take up offers from other clubs but, in total, 37 of them - or 62% - are not currently in management.

For most managers, it's rarely the case where you walk into a new club within a few weeks of leaving your last one, so what do out-of-work managers do between jobs to make sure they are ready to take the next opportunity that fits?

Known as 'The Bald Eagle', Jim Smith was renowned as a master of winning promotion during a management career that spanned almost 40 years. He is pictured here celebrating after leading Derby into the Premier League in 1996

It is more than 32 years since I received my marching orders from my first job at Bournemouth , who were in what is now known as League One. I was devastated.

I had - as I always did - given everything I could do to benefit the club, and with it being my first sacking I honestly did not know where my next step would take me.

But, on the second day of me being out of work, my home phone rang and at the end of the line was Jim Smith, who was in charge of Portsmouth, a few miles down the south coast.

I knew Jim then, but not really well. I'd been a manager for two years, but by then he had already spent 25 years in the dugout, at eight different clubs.

He asked how I was and, before I could even reply, recited these immortal words, which always stuck with me - "son, you're not a real manager until you get sacked at least three times - so get your backside off the sofa and get on with getting another job" - then he put the phone down!

I've used that sentence myself many times since to managers who have lost their job and are struggling to come to terms with it.

That can happen a lot. People outside the game maybe don't realise how difficult it can be when you are sacked, and how it affects certain individuals differently - you can easily fall off the merry-go-round and, as a manager, you never know for sure whether you will get another chance.

Bruce Rioch only spent one season at Arsenal but was responsible for bringing a certain Dennis Bergkamp to Highbury from Inter Milan, making the legendary Dutch striker his first signing in June 1995

Someone else who phoned me up in the summer of 1994 was another great name in the game as a player and manager, Bruce Rioch.

At the time, Bruce was having a lot of success as manager of Bolton - he would get the Arsenal job a few months later - and he asked me if I would scout for him while I was trying to find my next manager's post.

He was very keen to get me involved and very helpful in keeping me busy watching games.

I was equally keen on helping Bruce and ended up scouting for him for that entire season. To this day, I owe him so much in respect of what he asked me to do, because of what I learned during that time.

Football is the best team sport in the world and the fundamental thing I picked up that season is that its 'product', the players, were the secret to success.

By that, I mean that I realised that at all levels there are good players, and at all levels there are managers working on budgets. I learned that knowing the level you were at, and placing the right players at that level who you could afford, would be an enormous factor in your chances of success, or failure.

Yes, there is more to it than that - you then also had to pick good characters, coach them well and motivate them with a driving force they could handle and enjoy - but you have to start by getting the right players for the level you are at.

The following summer, I was appointed manager of Gillingham, who had just finished 89th out of the 92 clubs across the top four divisions.

I was lucky enough to inherit a club who had quite a few players out of contract, so it enabled me to reset the first team with several players I had watched during my time scouting for Bruce and Bolton.

All the hours and miles I travelled that year paid off, with Gillingham finishing second in what is now League Two and gaining promotion in my first season. Those players who we recruited kick-started four years of my managerial career in Kent, and left me with some fantastic on-field memories.

Napoleon (left) rose through the ranks to become the Emperor of the French as well as building a reputation as one of the great military commanders, and inspired Pulis (right) with his leadership skills

My time and success at Priestfield opened up an ever-revolving door of work and rest.

Whenever I was out of work in the years that followed, watching games still occupied my midweeks and weekends for the same reasons as before - I wanted to watch players who I might end up signing.

Lots of games I went to were watched from the terraces with either home or away supporters, which was always interesting and illuminating - I've always valued the views of match-going fans on different players.

Down the years, I was also invited to spend a few weeks coaching abroad, in Kuwait and the United States, by friends I had in the game.

Whatever I was doing, I always felt like I was learning, and not just by watching football around the world. I became an avid reader of sports books and also finding out about great leaders of men through history.

So, as well as visiting Bayer Leverkusen, Athletic Bilbao and RB Leipzig - who back then had only just started their rise from the bottom tier of German football - I would analyse and investigate historic battles or events.

Napoleon Bonaparte really kept me busy. His attention to detail and his command of his generals was only superseded by his troop's loyalty to him - they would literally die for him!

His 250th birthday was celebrated in Corsica in the summer of 2019, and a French newspaper invited me to go along and give a British perspective on how we see Napoleon as a leader and a person.

I was delighted to accept and was amazed by how many people from all over Europe turned up too.

Hated by many countries, but still adored by his followers, Napoleon also produced the Napoleonic Code, which is still the foundation of French civil law today.

The Charge of the Light Brigade was a disastrous assault by British cavalry led by Lord Cardigan against Russian forces during the Battle of Balaclava in 1854

As well as great military triumphs, I studied defeats too - they are as much a part of football management as victories, after all - and you can compare the organisational brilliance of Napoleon to the disaster of the Battle of Balaclava and the Charge of the Light Brigade.

One summer, I travelled out to Crimea to witness the scene of that tragic charge by the bravest of brave men.

Lord Raglan, the British commander-in-chief, was based on the high ground and could see everything in the Russian positions and the brigades.

His order to attack was ambiguous and although Lord Cardigan, who led the charge, questioned it, he still followed it through - leading to one of the most infamous military disasters in history.

It should never have happened but, just as in football, leadership and communication from the top was key. The instructions were passed down from Raglan to Lord Lucan to Cardigan and became garbled - too many cooks, in my opinion!

The last book which really stuck with me, in terms of inspiring me as a leader, was the story of HMS Endurance - disaster strikes during a journey through the ice fields of the southern hemisphere when the ship becomes stuck.

I cannot do justice to the deeds of Sir Ernest Shackleton in this column but his leadership of his men, along with his number two Frank Worsley, was extraordinary.

Both dovetailed in a way that gave their men the energy, desire and determination to believe and follow instructions in the most appalling conditions, never once questioning their leaders' abilities to help them survive.

Over the years, I've never stopped reading about, or watching, great leaders like that - there is so much that young coaches can learn from other sports or history that will benefit then, the same way it did me.

Going to games was still the most important thing when I was between jobs, because I would always believe my own eyes when watching players.

There were times when that became more of a challenge, especially at the back end of my career, but times change and if you are not in tune with what is happening in the game then you can get dropped very quickly.

But I am sure that most of my managerial compatriots would also agree with me that experience in all walks of life can be invaluable.

I learned so much when I was out of work, about all aspects of leadership, individually and collectively.

My advice to managers out of work now is the same that I received from Jim, all those years ago - pick yourselves up and get off the sofa to get back in work as quickly as possible.

You should never be afraid of dropping down a level the way I did, too. It is better to get a job, any job, than be out of football full-stop. That hasn't changed since my day, either.

Tony Pulis was speaking to BBC Sport's Chris Bevan.

Au was sentenced to 12 years and six months' jail for "subversion against the political power of the state"

Macau has sentenced an ex-lawmaker and pro-democracy campaigner to 12 years and six months' jail in the city's first national security case.

Following a closed-door trial, Au Kam San, 69, was convicted on Friday of "subversion against the political power of the state", among other offences.

His wife Virginia Cheang condemned the ruling, calling the case a "groundless persecution designed to humiliate Au".

Macau was handed back to China in 1999, ending over 400 years of Portuguese administration. Its national security law came into effect in 2009, criminalising acts of treason, secession, and subversion against the Chinese Communist Party.

The law was revised in 2023, broadening its scope to include non-violent acts of secession, and again this year, to allow for trials to be held behind closed doors.

Prosecutors had accused Au of assisting and collaborating with "external hostile organisations" by collecting, preparing and disseminating information that was "manifestly filled with political claims of a subversive nature against the state".

These took place "over a long period of time", the prosecutors claim.

Au was arrested in July 2025 and later charged with three counts of subverting the state's power, three counts of endangering national security by establishing contact with foreign organisations, and one count of breach of confidentiality.

He was found guilty of four of the seven charges following a three-day trial which ended in September. A judge had ordered that the trial be held behind closed doors "to ensure that no prejudice is caused to the interests of national security".

Macau's authorities never publicly disclosed the details of the case. Au's family had earlier told the media Au was not allowed to seek his own legal representation and had instead been assigned a lawyer by the court.

Au's wife Cheang said she hoped authorities would grant her and her family permission to regularly write to and visit Au in prison.

"I dare not hope for more as I believe that will only lead to greater disappointment," she said in an open letter on Friday.

Au, who was formerly a primary school teacher, was elected to the Legislative Assembly in September 2001. For 20 years, he served as one of only a handful of pro-democracy lawmakers in the legislature, largely made up of pro-Beijing loyalists.

Au had co-organised annual vigils in Macau to commemorate the 1989 Tiananmen Square crackdown in Beijing.

These vigils were previously tolerated in places like Macau and Hong Kong, but have effectively been banned in both cities since China imposed a sweeping national security law on Hong Kong in 2020.

Au's jailing comes a day after Hong Kong sentenced Joshua Wong, the face of its now-quashed democracy movement, to 10 years in jail . Wong, 30, whose activism started when he was just a teen, has been in custody for the last six years.
