Abacuruza imiti bo muri Kenya baburiye abagore ko badakwiye gushyira mu gitsina imiti ikoreshwa mu kuvura ubwivumbure bw'umubiri (allergie), bagamije kugikomeza cyangwa kugabanya ubugari bwacyo.

Uku kuburira kubaye nyuma y'uko ku mbuga nkoranyambaga hakwirakwijwe inama zishobora guteza ibyago bikomeye ku buzima bw'abagore.

Ubwo butumwa bwo ku mbuga nkoranyambaga bwavugaga ko umuti wa cetirizine, usanzwe ukoreshwa mu kuvura allergie kandi unyobwa unyuze mu kanwa, ushobora gutuma igitsina gikomera kurushaho, bikavugwa kandi ko kuwukoresha mu gitsina cy'abagore byongera ibyishimo mu gihe cy'imibonano mpuzabitsina.

N'ubwo rimwe na rimwe imiti ya antihistamine ishobora gutera kumagara (dryness) nk'ingaruka ku bayikoresha, impuguke zivuga ko ibyo bidasobanuye ko ishobora gukomeza imikaya y'igitsina.

Ihuriro ry'abacuruza imiti muri Kenya, bakaba banazobereye ibijyanye n'imiti, (Pharmaceutical Society of Kenya - PSK) ryavuze ko: "Kumagara mu gitsina bitavuze ko imikaya yegeranye bigaha igitsina gukomera. Ahubwo bishobora kongera uburyaryate, ububabare ndetse n'ibyago byo kwangirika kw'utunyangingo two mu gitsina."

Bongeyeho bati: "Gushyira iyo miti mu gitsina ntibitekanye. Ibinini bya cetirizine byakozwe kugira ngo binyobwe. Ibibigize ntabwo byigeze bipimwa ngo harebwe uko byagira ingaruka ku ruhu rworoshye rwo mu gitsina."

Cetirizine isanzwe ikoreshwa mu kugabanya ibimenyetso bya allergie nko kwitsamura, ibicurane, kuribwa amaso ndetse n'ibibazo by'uruhu.

Impaka ku gukoresha uyu muti mu gitsina cy'abagore, zatangiye mu ntangiriro z'iki cyumweru nyuma y'uko kuri TikTok hakwirakwiye ubutumwa buvuga ko cetirizine ishobora kugabanya ububobere bwo mu gitsina, bityo bikaba byatuma habaho kumva ko gikomeye kurushaho mu gihe cy'imibonano mpuzabitsina.

Amakuru ya BBC Gahuza ako kanya kuri WhatsApp yawe

Ibyo byateje impaka ndende, bamwe bashishikariza abandi kuyikoresha, mu gihe abandi bibazaga niba koko byaba byizewe.

Hari kandi amakuru yatangajwe n'itangazamakuru ryo muri Kenya avuga ko igiciro cy'uwo muti cyatangiye kuzamuka ndetse ko hari farumasi zimwe na zimwe, cyane cyane mu murwa mukuru Nairobi, zagaragaje ko abantu benshi bawushaka.

Mu itangazo yasohoye ku wa kane, PSK yagize iti: "Cetirizine ni umuti wa allergie unyobwa unyuze mu kanwa. Ntabwo wigeze wemezwa cyangwa ngo ugeragezwe ku kuwukoresha mu bundi buryo ubwo ari bwo bwose, cyane cyane kuwukoresha mu gitsina."

Yongeyeho iti: "Niba waramaze kuwukoresha muri ubwo buryo, hita ubihagarika. Niba ufite ububabare, kuva amaraso, kubabuka, kwishimagura, ibintu bidasanzwe bisohoka mu gitsina cyangwa umuriro, jya kwa muganga bagufashe."

PSK kandi yanasabye abakoresha imbuga nkoranyambaga n'ibyamamare bifite ababikurikira benshi (influencers) kwitondera amakuru y'ubuzima batangaza.

PSK yongeyeho ko kuvuga amakuru atari yo bishobora gushyira ubuzima bw'ababakurikira mu kaga, ndetse n'abaturage bose muri rusange.

PSK itanze ubu butumwa buburira, nyuma y'umunsi umwe gusa minisiteri y'ubuzima ya Kenya na yo igaragaje impungenge zayo ku bijyanye n'aya makuru yavugwaga kuri uwo muti, amaze iminsi akwirakwiza ku mbuga nkoranyambaga.

Ouma Oluga, umwe mu bayobozi bakuru mu rwego rw'ubuzima, yavuze ko hari abantu bamwe ku mbuga nkoranyambaga basa n'abafata nk'urwenya inama zitangwa n'impuguke mu buvuzi, batitaye ku ngaruka bishobora kubagiraho.

Yavuze kandi ko ubuyobozi bushobora gushyiraho uburyo bwo gukurikirana uko imiti itangwa n'uko igurwa, kugira ngo hafashwe gutahura aho yaba irimo gukoreshwa mu buryo butari bwo.

Gusa kugeza ubu nta cyemezo cya burundu kiratangazwa kuri icyo cyifuzo.

PSK yavuze ko izi amakuru avuga ko hari ubwiyongere bw'abashaka cetirizine, izamuka ry'ibiciro ndetse n'ibura ry'uwo muti, muri farumasi zimwe na zimwe.

Yasabye abacuruza imiti kutagendera kuri ayo makuru y'ibihuha ngo bashake guhenda abakeneye uwo muti, kuko bigenze bityo, abarwayi bawukeneye by'ukuri mu kuvura allergie bashobora gutangira kuwubura cyangwa banawubona ntibabashe kuwugura kubera kuwuhenda.

Iri huriro, ryanashishikarije abanyamuryango baryo kudatanga nkana imiti bazi neza ko igiye gukoreshwa nabi, kandi bagatangariza inzego z'ubuzima ingaruka mbi zaba zagaragaye ku bayikoresheje muri ubwo buryo.

PSK yasoje ubutumwa bwayo ivuga ko ibitangazwa ku mbuga nkoranyambaga bitaragenzuwe bidakwiye kurusha ijambo ibyo inzobere zivuga: "Banza ugishe inama umucuruzi w'imiti wabyigiye [cyangwa se umuganga], mbere yo gukoresha umuti uwo ari wo wose, kugira ngo utava aho uwukoresha mu buryo utagenewe."

Yunzemo iti: "Ntukizere ibivugwa ku mbuga nkoranyambaga mu gihe ushaka inama z'ubuvuzi."

MN202611_1phipxgbmea.t:
Phone First services direct patients to the most appropriate health service, depending on the severity of their condition - stock image

Northern Ireland's health minister has instructed trusts which have not yet stood down their Phone First service to "pause any planned cessation" of the scheme.

The telephone triage system has already been scrapped by the Belfast Trust; it was to end within weeks in the Northern Trust and is under review in the Western Trust.

Phone First is aimed at reducing unnecessary visits to hospital emergency departments (EDs) by providing advice to patients on appropriate care options.

In a statement to BBC News NI, the Department of Health (DoH) said health trusts that have not yet stood the service down will be "liaising with their external providers for an extension".

The Northern Trust's line was due to close on 27 November, but its interim chief executive, Suzanne Pullins said on Thursday that they have been told to "pause the formal withdrawal to allow for reassessment".

Pullins announced the development as she appeared before Stormont's Health Committee to answer questions about the trust's savings plans.

NI emergency departments to trial phone triage

Lagan Valley ED introduces 'phone first' service

GP telephone first system 'here to stay'

Last month, committee members had expressed concern that Phone First was being cut just as hospital EDs prepared to deal with increased winter pressures.

Pullins acknowledged those concerns on Thursday, saying the decision to stand it down was in "no way a reflection of the service" which was "very valued".

But she explained that there were "no easy choices" given the scale of the financial savings the trust had been asked to find.

Phone First costs £500,000 to run and the trust has been asked to make £53.8m in savings for this year.

The DoH statement said that the Belfast Trust had redeployed its Phone First staff "to urgent care services to secure access to Urgent and Emergency Care".

It added that all trusts are focused on supporting EDs "to ensure optimal patient flow and access to the right care in the right place at the right time and from the right clinician to meet the patient needs".

Phone First was initially introduced during the pandemic in late 2020 to reduce the risk of Covid-19 spreading among patients in crowded hospital waiting rooms.

Under the system, patients call a dedicate line before travelling to hospital to check if they really need to go to an ED or if they could be treated elsewhere

Operating in a similar manner the NHS's non-emergency 111 medical helpline in England, Scotland and Wales, it was designed to be used in urgent but not life-threatening cases - the public is still advised to always call 999 immediately if someone's life is at risk.

It was trialled in Causeway Hospital before being gradually rolled out across all five hospital trust areas.

However, it was run by five separate teams who each had different hours and different contact numbers.

Before it closed its line at the end of September, the Belfast Trust estimated that move would save it approximately £500,000.

Under the Phone First triage system, patients call a dedicated phone number to check if they really need to visit an emergency department

At last month's health committee meeting, senior staff from the Belfast Trust were questioned about their decision to cut the line as winter approached.

"It's frustrating, it's not something that we wanted to do... but we felt that it was the least worst option," said Claire Corry, Director of Finance at the Belfast Trust.

Her boss, Chief Executive Jennifer Welsh, explained the projected £800m shortfall in Northern Ireland's health budget meant all trusts had been instructed to find savings that "could be delivered without causing harm to service users".

Welsh explained Phone First was scrapped in Belfast in order to prioritise other services that "we think would generate more benefit for patients and staff".

She told Northern Ireland Assembly members at the 22 October meeting that there "wasn't a huge uptake in the service" and that it "wasn't having a huge impact".

However, Northern Ireland-wide statistics show a rising trend in usage over the past six years.

The Belfast Telegraph , external reported that calls reached their highest ever level in the same month that Belfast Trust closed its line.

The green bars represent calls which led to ED referrals and the shorter blue bars indicate calls in which patients were not advised to attend ED

There were 18,263 calls in September, 12,098 (66%) of which resulted in patients being referred on to EDs.

It was suggested to last month's committee that because two thirds of callers end up in EDs anyway, Phone First was less effective than some other services at reducing pressures.

But committee chair Philip McGuigan, of Sinn Féin, pointed out that Phone First may have helped to keep more than 6,000 callers out of ED in September alone.

During that meeting, McGuigan secured the support of the committee to write to the DoH to ask about the future of Phone First.

Before the minister announced the pause, BBC News NI had contacted all five trusts this week to ask about the future of their telephone triage services.

The Belfast Trust said its decision to stop its Phone First was taken "in the context of the very significant financial challenge" it and the wider health service was facing.

It added "other care options are still available" and pointed patients to its Choose the Right Care webpage in cases of urgent but non-life-threatening illness or injury.

The Western Trust said its Phone First service was being "assessed against current spend and affordability" as part of its savings plan.

"No decision has been made at this time and the service continues to operate as normal," its spokesperson added.

The South Eastern Trust said its Phone First service at both the Lagan Valley and Downe hospitals "will remain unchanged".

It added that Phone First is "not required" at the Ulster Hospital because its Urgent Care Centre directs patients "to the most appropriate service when they arrive".

A spokesman for the Southern Trust told BBC News NI it has no plans to withdraw Phone First.

MN202611_iifqly7o0k.t:
Wayne Rooney has transitioned to broadcasting following a managerial career with Derby County, DC United, Birmingham City and Plymouth Argyle

"I like a lot of them artists, but I thought it was crap."

Wayne Rooney's assessment of the 2026 World Cup final half-time show - delivered live on BBC Television - was blunt.

The show, which featured Madonna, BTS, Shakira and Justin Bieber, ran to 27 minutes and 22 seconds. Rooney, who played at three World Cups for England, was unimpressed.

It caught some - including fellow pundit Joe Hart - by surprise. But Rooney's plain-speaking and sense of humour through the tournament had connected with viewers.

On Thursday, the former Manchester United and England captain was named pundit of the year at the Broadcast Sport Awards. , external

Gabby Logan was named sports presenter of the year for her work across the World Cup, Six Nations, London Marathon, Match of the Day and European Athletics for BBC Sport.

Ed Leigh and Tim Warwood, who worked on Ski Sunday and the Winter Olympics, were given the sports commentator of the year award, while Ultras was named sports documentary of the year (series).

The awards were announced at a ceremony in London attended by 650 people from the sports television industry.

Rooney said: "I didn't realise how tough it was going to be when I first started doing it.

"I've always been my own biggest critic. And even now I need to improve, I need to be better. It's a lot of hard work."

Wayne wasn't holding back about the half-time show

Rooney's move to broadcasting after a stellar playing career - followed by a testing stint as a manager - has not always been smooth.

His debut as a full-time pundit on Match of the Day in August 2025 divided opinion, , external with one fan writing on social media: "Just because you have done something, does not automatically make you good to talk/explain and teach others well."

Guardian journalist Paul MacInnes was more upbeat about Rooney's debut.

"He's articulate, and on Saturday night was able to conjure up the right word when you could see he was looking for it," he wrote. , external

"He is tactically insightful and has a wealth of experience to draw from too."

As a player, Rooney learned from managers including Sir Alex Ferguson and David Moyes, and won the Champions League, Europa League, Premier League (five times), FA Cup and League Cup (three times).

He was not always the most articulate in his post-match interviews. As a pundit, he has found his voice.

In an attempt to better himself as a broadcaster, Rooney has sought feedback and advice from experienced television executives, as well as other players-turned-pundits including Alan Shearer, Danny Murphy, Hart and Micah Richards.

"I do look at the other pundits who have been there a long time," added Rooney.

"I see how they do it. I enjoy it, it keeps me involved in football."

Asked about dealing with criticism from people watching him on TV, Rooney responded: "You do see it.

"It drives me to be better. I always feel when I do something I want to do better and be the best I can."

Paul Stretford, Rooney's long-serving agent, said people should not be surprised by what his client can achieve.

"It is no surprise to me that Wayne has continued to put his doubters in their place with his football intelligence and straightforward manner," added Stretford.

"Time and time again as a player he was able to raise his game to incredible levels.

"They should also not be surprised at his drive and ambition to be the best that he can possibly be. And he does this with a combination of intelligence and humility."

Philip Bernie, head of BBC Sport events, said Rooney had shown a "great willingness to learn and determination to improve" as a broadcaster.

"Wayne is also a very likeable guy, a proper team player, with no ego on display," he added.

'One of the worst decisions I've ever seen' - Shearer & Rooney on Digne penalty shout

As well as developing chemistry with his fellow pundits, Rooney has changed his appearance after committing to a healthier lifestyle through a fitness regime which involves games of padel and boxing training.

"Like anyone who cares about their job, Wayne had to work hard - to learn skills around analysis and delivery - and he's improved so much in a short time," said Alex Kay-Jelski, director of BBC Sport.

"Micah and Joe alongside him at the World Cup were perfect team-mates - three equals - and you'll be seeing more of them together on the BBC in coming seasons."

Their chemistry was obvious in the summer, particularly when they swapped their microphones for oars after an erroneous Rooney prediction.

He pledged to row down the River Mersey if Norway beat Brazil, and when they did, he confirmed on air he would adapt the challenge to do it in the United States.

That led to him, Hart and Richards to take to the Hudson River in New York.

"Wayne deserves this so much," added Kay-Jelski. "He's a great mix of incredibly clever, funny in a self-deprecating manner and likeable.

"From a BBC side he's easy to work with, treats everyone the same whether they're a former team-mate or starting out in a junior position, and his words carry real weight."

MN202611_1xoud04n9gy.t:
One of the UK's smallest accredited zoos is celebrating after "extra special" pied tamarin twins were born at the site.

Shaldon Wildlife Trust, in Devon, said the critically endangered twins were born on 29 September to mum Bobby and dad Pedra. Its director, Zak Showell, said it was a "challenge" to breed the species.

The trust said the animals were among the most endangered primates in South America. Bosses said the infants were "thriving" and had started to hitch rides on their parents' backs as they explored their habitat.

Showell said: "For a zoo of our size to achieve this and to be one of just two European zoos to manage it this year is an unbelievable proud moment for our small team."

The trust said pied tamarins required "stress-free environments and specialist care"

"It has been an incredible year for births here at Shaldon, but these twins are extra special," he said.

"Pied tamarins are exceptionally delicate animals, and breeding them successfully is a challenge."

The trust said the primates required "stress-free environments and specialist care".

It said zoo keepers intentionally kept the news of the arrivals under wraps for a few weeks to give the "delicate family complete peace and quiet".

The species is listed as critically endangered on the International Union of Conservation and Nature's (IUCN) Red List.

The zoo said, in the wild, they were restricted to "a shrinking pocket of rainforest" around Manaus, Brazil.

MN202611_188zpvdsazb.t: Umukuru w’ubutumwa bw’Umuryango w’Abibumbye bwo kubungabunga amahoro muri Repubulika ya Demokarasi ya Congo (MONUSCO), James Swan, yahuriye i Goma n’uwahoze ari Perezida w’icyo gihugu Joseph Kabila, mu biganiro bya mbere bitangajwe ku mugaragaro bagiranye kuva Kabila agiye ku buyobozi bw’umutwe w’inyeshyamba wa FRN. MONUSCO yatangaje ko ibiganiro byabo byibanze kuri gahunda zikomeje zigamije kuzana amahoro, iyubahirizwa ry’agahenge hamwe no ku bikorwa bigamije kurangiza mu mahoro intambara yo mu burasirazuba bwa Repubulika ya Demokarasi ya Congo (DRC). Ubwo butumwa bwa ONU bwavuze ko Swan yanahuye n’abahagarariye itsinda rizwi nka MCVE+ rishinzwe kugenzura iyubahirizwa ry’agahenge, ashimangira ubufasha bwa MONUSCO kuri iyo gahunda, bijyanye n’inshingano za MONUSCO. Ubwo yaganiraga n’ibitangazamakuru byaho nyuma y’ibyo biganiro, Visi Perezida wa FRN Bertrand Bisimwa yavuze ko uwo mutwe ukiyemeje gukurikiza gahunda y’amahoro ya Doha. Ariko yanagaragaje impungenge ku ishyirwa mu bikorwa ry’amasezerano yagezweho muri ibyo biganiro by’i Doha muri Qatar. Bisimwa yakemanze gahunda zo kongerera igihe manda ya MONUSCO ndetse avuga ko FRN yifuza ko ubutumwa bwa MONUSCO bwakomeza kugenda bukurwa muri icyo gihugu gahoro gahoro, ari na ko bukomeza gukora inshingano zabwo mu gufasha mu igenzurwa ry’agahenge. Yanavuze ko icyifuzo cyo guhindura itegekonshinga rya DRC, muri gahunda yo gutuma Perezida Félix Tshisekedi yashobora kwiyamamariza manda ya gatatu, gishobora kugira ingaruka ku masezerano yagezweho muri gahunda ya Doha. Nta cyo leta ya DRC yahise itangaza kuri ayo magambo. Iyo nama yo ku wa kabiri ibaye mu gihe ibikorwa by’ubuhuza bwo mu karere no ku rwego mpuzamahanga bikomeje mu rwego rwo kubungabunga agahenge no gutuma ibiganiro by’amahoro bitera intambwe, hagamijwe kurangiza intambara imaze imyaka ibera mu burasirazuba bwa DRC. Ayandi makuru yacu mushobora kuyakurikira kuri YouTube kuri BBC News Gahuza Izindi nkuru wasoma: Kabila yatangajwe ko ari umukuru w'umutwe mushya w'inyeshyamba mu burasirazuba bwa RD Congo RD Congo : 'Ni ikimenyetso c'uko atigeze akunda igihugu', Tshisekedi kuri Kabila na FRN

MN202611_7fplxhm90j.t: Umusatirizi rurangiranwa wa Portugal mu mupira w'amaguru, Cristiano Ronaldo, yatangaje ko asezeye burundu gukinira umurwi nserukiragihugu. Uyu mukinyi w’imyaka 41, yaciye umuhigo kw’isi yose mu kwinjiriza Portugal ibitsindo 146 no gukina inkino 234 kuva atanguye gukinira igihugu ciwe mu 2003. Muri Nyakanga (9), Ronaldo yarivumbuye mu myiteguro y'umurwi serukiragihugu wa Portugal amaze kubwirwa ko atari gutanguzwa mu kibuga mu rukino rw’ihiganwa rya Nations League rwari guhuza Portugal na Danemark, ivyatumye acibwa ihadabu ry'amapawundi 215 hamwe no guhagarikwa mu kiringo c’imisi 30. Mu butumwa bwa videwo yashize kuri Instagram, Ronaldo yavuze ati: "Ku Banyaportugal, umunsi urashitse wo gusubiza inomero ndwi nahora nambara mu murwi nserukiragihugu. “Sinigeze numva ko iyo nomero yari iyanje jenyene, ariko mu myaka 23 nahawe amahirwe n'inshingano vyo kuyambara, kuyikingira no kuyinjirana mu bibuga bitandukanye kw'isi yose. “Uyu musi igihe kirageze co kuyiha urunganwe ruzokurikira. Si ingingo yoroshe gufata, kuko hari ingingo zidafatwa n'ubwenge gusa, ariko kandi zifatwa n'umutima. “Urugendo rwatanguye muri Myandagaro [8] 2003 rugahindura ubuzima bwanje burundu, ubu rurashitse kw'iherezo." Ishirahamwe ry’umupira w’amaguru rya Portugal (PFF) ryavuze ko ridashobora kwakira ubu butumwa bwo gusezera uko nyene, ata cubahiro rihaye Ronaldo. Mw‘itangazo ryayo, PFF yagize iti: "Turipfuza cane gutegura no gufashanya mu buryo bwose bushoboka kugira ngo Cristiano Ronaldo ahabwe icubahiro gikwiye kubera urugendo rwiwe rw'akataraboneka mu mupira w'amaguru, aho abafana hamwe n'igihugu cose bazosubira kuronswa akaryo ko kumushimira no kunezerererwa ivyo yaduhaye." Ronaldo yakinye mw’ihiganwa ry’igikombe ca Buraya (Euro) incuro zitandatu. Portugal yarangije ihiganwa ari iya kabiri mu 2004, hanyuma itsindira igikombe mu 2016, gusa ikaba itigeze irenga igice ca kabiri gishira ica nyuma mw’ihiganwa ry’igikombe c’isi mu mwuga wiwe. Yabaye kizigenza w’umurwi nserukiragihugu kuva mu 2008, kandi yarafashije Portugal gutwara Nations League ya mbere mu 2019, hanyuma iriyongera mu 2025. Mukeba wiwe ruhebwa akaba n’umukinyi rurangiranwa wa Argentine, Lionel Messi, na we yasezeye ku mupira w'amaguru w'amakungu muri Gitugutu (10), mu birori vyuzuye ibigumbagumba vyabereye i Buenos Aires imbere y'abarenga 85.000 bari bitavye. Ayandi makuru ushobora gusoma kuri Ronaldo: Umutoza 'atinya kumusimbuza' – Ronaldo yagowe no kwigaragaza mu gihe ibindi bihangange byitwaye neza Portugal yoba itanguye guha umugongo Ronaldo ? Trump, wahoze ari rwiyemezamirimo n’umushoramari ukomeye mu by’ubwubatsi, kuri iyi manda ye ya kabiri yahinduye cyane imiterere y’ibiro bya perezida w’Amerika, cyane cyane yongeraho ibice byinshi bikoze muri zahabu. Ku wa kane, Trump yabwiye abanyamakuru ati: “Turimo kubihindura urwibutso rw’igihugu, kandi ntibizemerwa ko bikorwaho [bihindurwa] n’umuntu uwo ari we wese, bisenywe, bishyirwe hasi n’abantu b’ibicucu, mu rwego rwo kubaka ikintu mu buryo bw’imiterere itandukanyeho gato.” Trump asinye iryo tegeko hashize amezi asenye igice cyose cyitwa East Wing cy'ibiro bye bya White House, uwo mushinga ukaba wararezwe mu nkiko. Uwo mushinga ntiwanemejwe n’inteko ishingamategeko y’Amerika. Imirimo y’ubwubatsi yarakomeje, hakaba hari gahunda zo guhindura icyo gice kikaba ahandi hantu hashya hakorerwa ibirori n’iminsi mikuru. Iryo tegeko teka, Trump yashyizeho umukono ku wa kane, ritangaza ko icyumba perezida akoreramo – Oval Office – ari urwibutso rw’igihugu, hamwe n’ibindi byumba bimwe na bimwe bigikikije. Trump yagize ati: “Dukunda Oval Office, kandi ni ikirango, cyo kimwe na White House ubwayo. Ni ikirango cy’igihugu cyacu n’ubuhangange bw’igihugu cyacu.” Yongeyeho ko abategetsi bo hirya no hino ku isi bamusuye mu mezi ya vuba aha ashize bamushimiye ku bw’izo mpinduka yakoze kuri icyo cyumba. Trump yavuze ko White House na Oval Office byari bimaze igihe bicyeneye gusanwa mbere yuko akora izo mpinduka, avuga ko ibyo biro byari “byarangiritse cyane”. US President Donald Trump has signed an executive order that he says will prevent future presidents from making certain changes to the White House Oval Office.

The executive order declares the president's official office, which he has renovated, to be a national monument.

"We're making it a national monument, and it will not be allowed to be touched by anybody, destroyed, ripped down by stupid people, in order to build something in a slightly different shape," Trump told reporters on Thursday.

The order does not prevent future presidents from changing the decor of the famous room.

The document says that it does not "restrict the President's authority to redecorate the monument, select furnishings, or make ordinary operational and security modifications that do not substantially impair the monument's historic structure or architectural character".

American presidents currently have the power to make some changes to the White House but large projects require the permission of Congress.

The order comes months after Trump tore down the entirety of the White House East Wing in a project that has faced legal challenges.

The project was not approved by the US Congress. Construction has continued, with plans to turn the space into a new ballroom.

How Trump is remaking the White House in his own image

Signing the new executive order on Thursday, the president said: "We like the Oval Office, and it's a symbol, like the White House itself. It's a symbol of our country and the greatness of our country."

He added that world leaders who have visited in recent months have complimented his decorative changes to the room.

Trump said the White House and the Oval Office had been in need of repairs before his changes, calling it "badly damaged". He described broken windows, cracked walls and broken stone.

Many of the noticeable changes, though, were cosmetic, including a large gold plaque reading "Oval Office" outside the space, paving over the Rose Garden and adding a new helicopter pad.

Trump said the order would "make it impossible for anybody ever to destroy this incredible space".

The Oval Office in 2025 during Trump's second term in the White House

The Oval Office in 2024 during Joe Biden's tenure

The office in 2015 during Barack Obama's time in the White House

It is unclear whether this action could simply be reversed by a future president or a legal challenge.

Most executive orders can be overturned and Trump himself scaled back two national monuments in Utah in 2017. But revoking a national monument designation has not yet been tested in court.

The White House grounds are already designated as a National Historic Landmark, which is intended to prevent against sudden changes to the building.

Trump's order calls on the Oval Office to be maintained by the National Park Service "in a manner that protects its historic character, architectural integrity, and association with the Presidency".

It notes the existing protections to the White House, but says "nonetheless, the Oval Office merits specific recognition and protective management as a discrete historic structure of national significance".

Congress has carved out an exemption to the National Historic Preservation Act, in order to allow presidents to make needed changes. The current Oval Office has existed since the early 1930s, after its conception by President Franklin D Roosevelt.

Greg Werkheiser, from the law firm Cultural Heritage Partners, which specialises in historic preservation, says that temporary alterations like "furniture and decor is completely up to the president's discretion".

"As long as they're not damaging the permanent art and architecture, they can generally do whatever they want," he told the BBC.

A new gold sign was placed outside the Oval Office

A Trump administration staff member seen inside the Oval Office in May

Werkheiser argues that the Trump administration has shown disregard for other historic sites in Washington and, through lawsuits, has attempted to undermine the laws that require preservation.

He called Trump's order "hypocrisy", noting the various projects he's pushed for across Washington - including plans to build a new triumphal arch, which has been temporarily put on hold by a federal judge.

"On the one hand he's talking about the importance of preserving the Oval Office - which is legally meaningless because he can't do it - and on the other hand he is absolutely taking an axe to the law that allows us to preserve other historic sites."

Trump's massive arch wins approval as protesters threaten to block it

Global stock markets have tumbled after investors sold tech shares on fears that the US midterm elections would slow the development of artificial intelligence (AI).

The sell-off, which started in the US and then spread to Asia and Europe, has seen trillions of dollars wiped off the stock value of major tech firms.

In the US, the tech-heavy Nasdaq share index sank 5.5% on Thursday. Asian markets also saw hefty falls on Friday and European markets opened lower.

Investors are worried about tougher regulation of AI, after Democrat candidates opposed the data centres needed by the technology. The share falls also come on top of concerns about whether the huge amounts being spent on AI will pay off.

The sell-off in US stocks meant the so-called magnificent seven tech companies, including Apple, Nvidia and Tesla, shed a trillion dollars in value in a single trading day, with Nvidia shares sliding more than 9%.

Shares in Elon Musk's companies SpaceX and Tesla also plunged, falling 8% and nearly 11% respectively and shaving more than $300bn off the firms' market value.

Musk had spent nearly $450m backing Republican campaigns, including at least $45m in support of Ken Paxton for the Texas senate seat, but Texas turned blue in the Democratic tsunami on Tuesday.

The sharp fall in the Nasdaq meant it lost an estimated $2.5tn (£1.9tn) in market value. The index is now in what market watchers call correction territory, which is where an index or company value falls at least 10% below its recent high.

However, the huge gains seen by tech stocks in recent times - driven by the enthusiasm for AI - mean that even after Thursday's fall, the Nasdaq is still higher than it was a year ago, and up about 4.6% from where it was at the start of this year.

The US sell-off spread into Asia on Friday. The Nikkei share index in Japan closed down 6% as shares in memory chip makers Kioxia and Tokyo Electron saw big falls.

In South Korea, the Kospi index plunged more than 8% at one point, triggering a so-called circuit breaker, a mechanism that temporarily halts trading to curb panic selling.

The Kospi eventually closed down 6%, with shares in chipmaker SK Hynix falling more than 10%.

European markets fell on Friday, although the declines were not as severe as the indexes contain fewer tech stocks. The UK's FTSE 100 index fell nearly 2% while Germany's Dax index was down 2.4%.

Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, said investors were worried about the huge amounts of money being spent on AI with "no clear idea of when, or whether, there will be payback".

"The midterm election result muddied the waters as the Democrats now have more influence and could slow down the pace of data centre roll-outs and look at new ways to regulate the sector," he added.

"The AI story has all been about speed, and now there is a danger of it moving to a lower gear, and some of the wheels falling off."

Democrats in races across the US campaigned to slow the growth of data centres and AI, and there were dozens of measures on ballots around the country aimed at restricting the development of the hubs crucial for powering the technology.

They won both the US Senate and House of Representatives in the midterms, taking control of Congress for the rest of President Donald Trump's presidency.

"Americans don't want Big Tech oligarchs wrecking the environment, gutting jobs and threatening humanity's future. NATIONAL DATA CENTER MORATORIUM NOW," Bernie Sanders, an Independent Senator who often votes with the Democrats, said in a post on X on Thursday.

How does it affect me if share prices fall?

These firms you've never heard of are feeding fears the AI bubble could burst

Food, fuel and taxes – can the Democrats actually make life cheaper?

Trump blamed the stock slide on his political opponents.

"The Stock Market suffered one of the Worst Days in History based on the results of the Election," he said in a social media post on Thursday.

"Remember, it wasn't Republicans, it was Dumocrats."

He also appeared to take aim at voters too.

"The Stock Market crashed today because the Dumocrats had a big Tuesday — So sad to see, you only have yourselves to blame!" he wrote on Truth Social.

On Friday, Trump restated his support for the AI sector, saying only "foolish leadership" would "say no to the riches they bring".

A backlash over data centres is another threat to the AI juggernaut

Big, noisy and coming to a town near you - why the data centre backlash is growing

Some tech leaders have said they were caught off guard by the backlash against data centres in the midterms.

OpenAI president and co-founder Greg Brockman said he believed everyone had been surprised by the reaction to data centres, and more work needed to be done to ensure communities were on board.

"A lot of our shift over the course of this year has really been to realise that from San Francisco trying to build infrastructure in Texas, Georgia, and other places, you can't just tweet and say: 'This is going to be good.' You need to be in those communities," Brockman said at the WSJ Tech conference in Napa, California.

With additional reporting from Lily Jamali

Correction 9 November: This story was amended to state that Bernie Sanders is an Independent Senator and not a Democrat

Brand found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault

Russell Brand has been convicted of rape and sexual assault, and is now expected to face a substantial prison sentence.

A jury found the entertainer guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault, following a four-week trial at Southwark Crown Court in London.

He was found not guilty of two other counts of rape, and one count of attempted indecent assault. The jury deliberated for eight-and-a-half hours.

The 51-year-old was refused bail and will spend the weekend in custody before he is due to return to the same court on Monday for sentencing.

It can now be reported that Brand is also facing further rape allegations made by two women and has already been questioned by officers in relation to the complaints. The Metropolitan Police said its investigation "remains ongoing".

During the trial, Brand faced allegations from six women spanning the decade between 1999 and 2009, when he rose to fame as one of Britain's most high-profile entertainers.

The women came to court to reveal how Brand used his immense fame to force them into sexual activity.

Brand, who told his wife Laura Brand "I love you" after entering the dock, displayed no emotion as the jury delivered its verdicts.

Afterwards he mouthed "I'm good, I'm good" to his defence counsel as he left the dock. His walk was steadily paced, and he continued to show little emotion.

The judge, Mr Justice Bennathan, told Brand to expect "a significant custodial term" after the verdicts were delivered.

How the outspoken comedian went from Hollywood stardom to a prison sentence.

Brand was denied bail and taken into custody after the verdicts, with sentencing due on Monday

The jury found Brand guilty of raping a fan after meeting her at a 2009 stand-up show at the Hammersmith Apollo.

Brand was found guilty of groping an MTV worker during a party at a Soho bar in 2004, but not guilty of going on to rape her in a toilet.

He was convicted of kissing and groping a Choice FM worker after encountering her in a corridor at the Capital Radio building in 2004 or 2005.

Brand was also convicted by the jury of sexually assaulting a Channel 4 worker in 2009 when she had been forced to give him a massage.

Brand was found not guilty by the jury of raping a woman he met at a cabaret show on the fringes of the 1999 Labour Party conference in Bournemouth.

He was also cleared of trying to drag an MTV worker in to a toilet to indecently assault her in 2001.

Brand was pictured arriving at court on Thursday with his wife Laura Brand before the verdicts were delivered

Brand was taken into custody following the verdicts and Laura Brand left court shortly afterwards

Brand had claimed to be the victim of a media conspiracy to paint him as a sexual predator and insisted in court that consent was "more important than sex itself".

But he faced the compelling evidence of six women who accused him of crimes over the course of a decade.

Brand was also confronted with his own words from his 2007 book in which he claimed sex was a "birthright" and friends who revealed his relentless pursuit of sleeping with 5,000 women.

Mr Justice Bennathan ruled that Brand must be remanded into custody until sentencing on Monday, when he is expected to receive a lengthy prison sentence.

The judge said "I regret the hardship caused to the children, of course" after being told that Brand would like bail over the weekend to explain the convictions to his children.

But he said Brand "has considerable resources", adding: "Whatever the good intentions of the family and the defendant today, I think there are substantial grounds to fear he might in the end not feel able to come along and face his sentence."

Brand faced further questioning from officers in July 2025

Get the latest news and analysis on BBC podcast Russell Brand on Trial - available on BBC Sounds, YouTube, iPlayer, or wherever you get your BBC podcasts

After the verdict, Detective Superintendent Andy Furphy paid tribute to the "extraordinary courage, resilience and determination of the women who came forward and reported what happened to them".

"Despite intense media and public scrutiny, they relived deeply personal and traumatic experiences and placed their trust in us. Without their bravery, this outcome would not have been possible," he said.

"Brand used his influence, status and fame to exploit and sexually offend against women. As his profile grew, so too did his sense of entitlement."

He added: "I hope this conviction sends a clear message that no one is above the law, no matter how famous or powerful they may be."

David Roberts, senior crown prosecutor in the London rape and serious sexual assault unit, described Brand as "predatory".

"He was a manipulator with an insatiable desire to get what he wanted regardless of whether consent was given or not," he said.

"As his career took off, he seized opportunities to assault the women around him. Although his tactics varied, at the centre of every assault was an abuse of power and sexual greed, with a complete disregard for the impact of his actions.

Ron Brand, Russell's father told the BBC he was "bemused and shocked" by the verdicts, adding: "I just didn't expect this - it's wrong... it's devastating."

In his evidence, Brand admitted using his fame to "facilitate sexual access" and being "obsessed" with sex and "extremely promiscuous" in the past.

He said he had "dedicated a lot of my life to what seems now beyond reckless, philandering, and idiocy".

But he insisted the sex was always consensual, and he denied all the charges.

His barrister told jurors that Brand "had an immense amount of sex", but that "none of it was unlawful".

Court sketches portrayed Laura Brand looking on as her husband was convicted

Allegations about Brand's behaviour first emerged in the media in September 2023.

The Times, Sunday Times and Channel 4's Dispatches programme jointly reported that four women had accused him of rape, sexual assault and emotional abuse - claims he strongly denied.

The investigation into other reports against Brand began soon after the story broke.

Brand first rose to fame as a stand-up comedian and became a household name as host of TV shows such as Big Brother's Big Mouth, and with his own radio programmes on stations including BBC Radio 2 and 6 Music.

He went on to establish a Hollywood career, starring in films including Forgetting Sarah Marshall and Get Him To The Greek. He was married to pop star Katy Perry from 2010 to 2012.

In recent years he has reinvented himself as an online social, political and religious commentator.

Channel 4, The Times and Sunday Times and the BBC all paid tribute to the women involved in the case, highlighting their "courage".

Channel 4, which aired Big Brother and its spin-off programmes at the time Brand was a presenter, said it recognised the "profound impact of these crimes".

The Times and The Sunday Times also paid tribute to women who took part in their investigation with Channel 4 but who did not have their cases brought before a court, saying their contributions had been "vital".

A BBC spokesperson said there could be "no place for the abuse of power" and added: "Across the industry we must work together to ensure that anyone who suffers at someone else's hand feels able to report it, that their concerns are taken seriously and that they are listened to."

The corporation restated its apology to staff who felt they could not speak up with concerns about Brand's behaviour when he worked at the BBC between 2006 and 2008, because he was seen as "too influential".

As it happened: Russell Brand found guilty of rape and three sexual assaults

The White House has denied rumours that Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth and Secretary of State Marco Rubio might leave their jobs in a post-election shakeup of the Trump administration.

US media have reported there are calls to replace Hegseth - in particular over his handling of the Iran war, which is being blamed for heavy Republican election losses.

One outgoing congressional Republican has threatened to force an impeachment vote against Hegseth as early as next week. The defence secretary posted a video statement defending his record and denouncing the effort.

"You see, they attack me. They attack us because we are effective," he said. "It's not going to work. We will not back down."

Vance walks Trump tightrope with scathing election critique blaming Iran war

Meanwhile, Rubio is denying reports he is considering leaving his post ahead of a 2028 presidential run.

Working for Trump until the end of his term has "always been my plan," Rubio told The New York Times in an interview.

"I love the work I'm doing," Rubio said. "And plus I always laugh when they say he's going to leave his job. I go, 'Which one?'"

The White House and US State Department also shut down reports that Rubio might be leaving after this week's midterm losses, with both calling it "fake news".

The defence secretary, though, faces a more uncertain political future.

Trump and Vice-President JD Vance have both blamed the Iran war for Republican losses that allowed Democrats full control of the US House of Representatives and the Senate.

In a telephone interview with ABC News, Trump said that he had received "calls about" Hegseth, but added that he had "every intention" of keeping him.

Later on Thursday, he told reporters at the White House that "Pete Hegseth has done a fantastic job", and went on to list what he sees are some of his achievements, including the arrest of Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro in January and the Iran war, now into its ninth month.

The Washington Post reported on Thursday that Trump might be, however, considering ousting General Dan Caine, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, or Centcom chief Admiral Brad Cooper. Both played significant roles in offering guidance on the war, which started eight months ago.

Meanwhile, Republican Representative Thomas Massie, a frequent critic of Trump, has said he will push ahead with plans to push for Hegseth's impeachment.

He told news site Politico that he will trigger his resolution to impeach the defence secretary early next week.

And on X, he warned that the president should replace Hegseth before a new Democratic-controlled Congress forms in January.

"He should do it while he can still get the replacements confirmed in the Senate," Massie wrote on X.

Could Democrats in Congress end the war in Iran?

Hegseth has also been rumoured to be interested in running for an open Tennessee Senate seat.

In his video statement, Hegseth denounced the "sham articles of impeachment" effort against him from a "disgruntled, defeated congressman, along with all his Democrat allies", and listed ways the department has fulfilled Trump's America First agenda under his leadership.

That includes, he said, reviving military recruitment, rebuilding the defence industrial base, and rooting out diversity initiatives.

Of the Democrats, he said: "Their policies don't work. So their obsession with political theatre disguised as power drives them to try to destroy their opponents. It's all about the politics of personal destruction."

Equity Bank Rwanda has launched EMMA, a digital wallet app that lets users make payments, send and receive money, save towards personal goals and, if eligible, access credit.

The platform was introduced at an exclusive soft launch for media and creatives, who got to try it out, test everyday transactions and share feedback. Guests explored how EMMA works for shopping, sending money, making payments, saving and accessing eligible credit.

EMMA connects to Rwanda’s interoperable payments network, including eKash, MTN MoMo, Airtel Money and participating banks.

Customers can register with an active mobile number and accepted identification; they do not need an existing Equity Bank account.

They can use the app or, on supported networks, dial *555*6#. Assistance is available through Equity Bank branches and agents.

Selected transactions carry no fee, including transfers between EMMA users or to Equity accounts, payments at PWE tills or eKash-connected merchants, deposits through approved agents and airtime purchases.

Many everyday transactions are free, while supported transfers to other banks and mobile wallets cost RWF 20.

At the November 5 launch in Kigali, Managing Director Hannington Namara said Rwanda had made progress in helping people move money, but the next step was ensuring that access improves their lives.

“Our next responsibility is to help that money move lives forward,” he said.

Diane Uwase, a Kigali-based small business owner, said the wallet could make everyday business payments easier. “Before EMMA, I often had to wait until I could get to a bank to handle payments. Now I can send and receive money from my phone, which makes running my business easier.”

Namara cited FinScope 2024 figures showing that 96% of Rwandan adults are financially included, while 22% hold a bank account and 10% are considered financially healthy.

He said EMMA’s success should be measured by active use and stronger saving habits, “not by downloads alone.”

The bank says customer transaction activity may help assess eligibility for overdrafts and short-term loans, subject to approval and disclosed terms.

Nithya Raman, once seen as a long-shot candidate, will be LA's new mayor

Democratic socialist Nithya Raman has toppled incumbent Karen Bass in the race for mayor of Los Angeles.

Raman's win stunned political watchers in California after she entered the race as a long-shot candidate against Bass, a political heavyweight who previously served in Congress and had never lost a race for political office.

Raman has frequently been compared to New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani. Both are democratic socialists and ran on progressive platforms.

Her win solidifies that America's two biggest cities will now be led by democratic socialists, which include some of the most high-profile politicians in the US, such as Mamdani and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.

Los Angeles was always likely to have a Democratic mayor but the question in the city - the second most populous city in the US - was just how left voters would be willing to go.

Bass, also Democrat, announced that she had called and conceded to Raman in a post on social media on Thursday, writing "while this is not the outcome we hoped for, the people of Los Angeles have spoken."

"Moving this city forward is what Los Angeles needs from all of us," Bass wrote. "I love Los Angeles. I believe in Los Angeles. And I will continue to ensure the promise of a better life belongs to all of us."

Boebert, billionaires' tax and other midterms races still to watch

Food, fuel and taxes – can the Democrats actually make life cheaper?

'This is a disaster': Angry Republicans blame Trump for midterms defeat

Raman, a member of city council and Indian immigrant, ran on a platform of change and fixing the "broken status quo and the politicians who failed them over and over again".

She ran on cutting homelessness, increasing housing in the city, saving Hollywood jobs from continued cuts and protecting residents from immigration enforcement efforts. Raman also vowed to fix the city's many issues, including helping beautification efforts, fixing roads and even helping bring back nightlife in the city.

The major issue in the race, however, was the LA fires, which killed dozens of people and razed neighbourhoods across the area in 2025. Bass faced intense political fallout over her absence during the emergency and the city's response to the disaster.

The next mayor in LA will oversee hosting the Super Bowl in 2027 and the 2028 Summer Olympics.

Watch: Mamdani says he's a democratic socialist. What does that mean?

Raman entered the race as a long-shot candidate but slowly shored up support, especially from younger voters, before besting reality star Spencer Pratt in the primary race earlier this year.

Raman's win over Bass has all the appearances of echoing voter sentiment across the US as part of sweeping Democratic wins, including in deep-Republican country that hadn't seen liberal leaders in decades.

Washington DC also elected democratic socialist Janeese Lewis George as its new mayor, furthering progressive leadership in another major US city.

US President Donald Trump was asked at the White House about the wins by politicians on the left flank of the Democratic Party and said, "If you go by history, it's going to be a disaster".

Such candidates have become a focal point of attacks by Republicans.

Bass had been a prominent member of Congress before becoming LA's first black female mayor. Her roots are closely tied to LA and its history, even working as a community organiser during the violent 1992 riots over police brutality in the beating of Rodney King, who was black.

High above the Arctic, powerful winds usually circle the North Pole each winter, helping trap some of the coldest air on Earth.

But this circulation, known as the polar vortex, has weakened and shifted position in recent days.

While such disruptions can occur during winter, scientists say an event this early in November is unprecedented in modern observations.

Similar disruptions in past years have sometimes been followed by colder weather affecting parts of Europe and North America.

However, as this is happening so early in the season, there are few historical examples to compare with and it could throw current winter forecasts into even more uncertainty.

The polar vortex develops every autumn as temperatures fall in the Arctic.

Strong westerly winds form in the stratosphere, roughly 10 to 30 miles (15-50km) above Earth's surface, locking the coldest air near the pole.

Atmospheric disturbances can cause the air high up to start warming which then makes the vortex winds weaken. This sudden stratospheric warming (SSW) can eventually lead to the strong westerlies reversing into easterly winds.

In the following days and weeks these changes can alter the position of the jet stream, increasing the chance of a blocked weather pattern where it can become drier with a colder northerly or easterly wind bringing Arctic air in.

It can also boost the possibility of snow, especially in eastern UK.

Most SSW events tend to occur from mid-winter but we are currently witnessing a dramatic weakening of the strong winds with some forecasts even showing a reversal of the polar vortex winds by mid-November.

Due to this weakening, the vortex has stretched and briefly split into two smaller circulations around the Arctic.

Sudden stratospheric warming can lead to a weakening of the polar vortex, resulting it in becoming disrupted, even split, high above the Arctic region

If the winds continue to weaken and end up reversing as forecast, this will be known as a major SSW event.

Jeff Knight, lead climate scientist from the Met Office, told the BBC: "It would appear to be the earliest on record looking back over the 75 years we've been observing…with most experts agreeing this is a very unusual event."

The current earliest major SSW event occurred on 28 November in 1969 and 2025.

Reasons for why we're seeing such an early event is not clear. It could be just part of the variability of our weather patterns.

But we also know in a "normal" El Niño year, this can typically bring a weakening of the polar vortex towards the end of winter.

While the warmer waters of the Pacific in an El Niño directly disrupt the weather around tropical areas, pulses of energy in the atmosphere, known as planetary waves, can cause disturbances even at polar regions.

These waves can push the polar vortex out of position and break the circulation up.

With the current record El Niño taking us into uncharted territory in terms of disruption to worldwide weather patterns, Knight suggested it could have "helped load the dice for this SSW event. However, because this is so rare, there's not enough evidence".

A link between a strong El Niño and early onset of a SSW event is unclear and will need further research.

Long-range forecasts issued by the Met Office show that the UK was more likely to see a stormy start to winter, followed by a colder spell to end winter. This is consistent with expectations from an El Niño pattern.

However, this unusually early SSW event was not widely expected.

Professor Andrew Charlton-Perez, meteorologist at the University of Reading, said: "The typical response to a SSW is for colder and drier conditions over Europe and the UK."

"Because we haven't seen a SSW event quite like this before, it is harder to anticipate a cold spell at the moment."

The Arctic is not yet as cold as it becomes later in winter, with the polar vortex itself having only recently developed.

Any influence it may have on weather patterns could be weaker than during a mid-winter disruption.

And because the air isn't at mid-winter temperatures yet it means cold and snowy weather for the UK is far from guaranteed.

While snow is not likely in the coming weeks, a possible continuation of drier than average conditions will be concerning for replenishment of our reservoirs

Long-term forecasts are based on large-scale climate signals and how they have affected weather patterns in previous years.

Much of the forecast for this autumn and winter has been focused around the influence of the exceptionally strong El Niño, pointing to a stormier start to winter, with the potential to be followed by colder and drier conditions from January.

But this unusually early disruption of the polar vortex and SSW presents meteorologists with a situation for which there are few modern comparisons.

For Charlton-Perez, the "concerning thing would be if this event ends up bringing the typical drier weather pattern and lack of rain" associated with a sudden stratospheric warming over the coming months.

With most of England and Wales still in drought, we need to rely on a wetter winter to fill up extremely low reservoirs.

For now, experts stress that it is too early to know whether recent changes in the polar vortex will change the winter outlook.

Stormy autumn, cold winter - how might El Niño affect the UK weather?

U2 speaking to BBC News in Dublin, 2026 (L-R): Larry Mullen Jr, Edge, Bono, Adam Clayton

U2 are at their best when they act on instinct.

Their biggest songs are fuelled by fiery indignation (Pride, Sunday Bloody Sunday) or sudden inspiration (One, Sometimes You Can't Make It On Your Own).

When they overthink, they misfire. An attempt to marry grunge and hip-hop on the 2009 single Get On Your Boots was, in the words of drummer Larry Mullen Jr, "a catastrophic choice".

So it was a good sign when, at the start of 2026, the band rushed out two EPs of new music, ripped from the headlines of a world in turmoil.

The first, Days of Ash, was urgent and angry – addressing the shooting of US citizen Renee Good by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer; and the death of Palestinian activist Odeh Hathaleenm, who was allegedly killed by an Israeli settler. ( Yinon Levy has been charged with reckless manslaughter and said he would fight for his innocence in court. )

U2's follow-up, Easter Lily, was more reflective, asking whether faith and friendship are enough to sustain us in challenging times.

Together, they were the band's strongest material in years, combining the combustive power of their early, post-punk incarnation with the melodic sophistication they developed in the late 1980s.

"We put those EPs out without telling anyone," says Bono, the band's voluble frontman.

"Our management, our label, they all said, 'You can't do that, people won't notice'.

"And we said, 'We don't mind. It's okay not to have a big hype behind everything'.

"And it was really beautiful. The people who we wanted to notice, noticed."

For long-term U2 watchers, that's a big shift.

This is the group who described their 2000 album All That You Can't Leave Behind as the sound of four men "re-applying for the job of biggest band in the world"; and who forced 2014's Songs of Innocence into 500 million people's iTunes libraries - an epic act of overreach that Bono's been apologising for ever , external since , external .

U2's first big break was winning a talent show in Limerick in 1978 - earning £500 and the chance to record their own music

There's no such hoopla around their new album, Carnaval de Luz, which is getting a pretty traditional roll-out for one of the world's biggest rock bands.

Sure, there's the requisite deluge of box sets and vinyl variants, a filmed concert for BBC Two , and a handful of interviews, including this one. But, more than ever, U2 want the music to speak for itself.

The album's a companion piece and a counterbalance to Days of Ash and Easter Lily. Inspired by ecstatic nights at music festivals, it rejects anxiety in favour of what Bono calls "defiant joy".

There's a stirring ballad titled If The World Is at War, We Better Not Be; while the chiming guitars of Superficiality lend an optimism to Bono's affirmation that, "the news can't break us".

"We didn't want to be dragged down by dark clouds or melancholy," explains bassist Adam Clayton.

"Our journey from the mid 1970s was about expanding freedom and opportunity for everyone: Make your own rules, pull down what wasn't useful. Now we seem to be in a period where that's under threat and under attack.

"We wanted to make the point that we didn't want our joy robbed."

During recording sessions last year, Bono told me U2 were chasing " the sound of the future ". In a separate interview with Radio 2's Jo Whiley, guitarist The Edge claimed they were working on an album of " sci-fi Irish folk" .

The electronic groove of the opening track, Go (Carnaval de Luz), echoes their experimental 90s phase; while the serrated riffs of Silencio are direct descendants of 2004's Vertigo.

U2 celebrate 50th anniversary at the school where they formed

The sci-fi folk idea persists, however, on the closing track Torn – a duet with Dolly Parton, that became the country star's last ever recording.

To court the first lady of country, Bono sent her a set of bagpipes for her birthday. Intrigued, she agreed to listen to his demos.

"We had some folk songs we were playing, there was one called Lifelong, and I remember her saying, 'You know, that's a little too Irish for me'," he recalls.

"So she said, 'Look, I've started a song called Torn. You can take it where you want, and I might like where you take it'.

Dolly Parton's song marks the transition point between Carnaval de Luz and the politically motivated songs of the Days of Ash EP

Parton's original lyric was about a woman trying to choose between two men but, with help from Snow Patrol's Jonny McDaid, U2 rewrote the song to address the political divisions tearing families apart.

" Brothers turn to strangers /And sons deny their name / Somebody loses either way And every heart is torn ."

Parton recorded her parts in June, less than three months before she died.

"We knew she was ill, but we had no idea that it'd be her last vocal," says Bono.

"That was a real shock. A shock for us because we'd been working with her, but a shock for anyone who loves music.

"I remember I was with [R.E.M. frontman] Michael Stipe in a car when the news came in, and he actually fell down and started sobbing. He just could not believe it.

"Probably the only thing that people can agree on in the entire world right now is Dolly Parton. Whether you're gay or straight or conservative or liberal, she was ready for you to fly at her show."

Another female presence shimmers on the fourth track, The Mirror Maker, which is dedicated to Catalan superstar Rosalía. Written after witnessing her spell-binding Lux tour , Bono describes the "heavens swirling" to reveal "the re-enchantment of the world".

"Normally you have to be dead or in jail for us to write a song about you," he laughs, "but she's a feminine force field. A kind of transcendent, ecstatic musician."

He wrote the song without her knowledge, phoning the singer afterwards to timidly seek her approval.

"It could have been excruciating if she really, really hated it," he grimaces. "I'd have had to pretend it was about Santa Rosalia, a saint who lived in a cave in Italy in the 17th Century."

Bono says the band are "relentless" when it comes to writing and recording new material

According to producer Jacknife Lee, The Mirror Maker went through 196 different takes before U2 were happy, suggesting they haven't entirely abandoned their perfectionist streak.

"The early sessions for this album were at times super inspiring, and then really not that good at all," admits The Edge, identifying a stubborn "stick-with-it-ness" that stops them from giving up.

"This band is absolutely relentless," agrees Bono. "It's a grudge match."

"It's the most frustrating thing," Mullen Jr adds. "I'm always reminded of how incapable I am of doing all those things that other people find easy.

"It's always been a challenge for us, and that's what makes those moments when it [works] so special. That's why you keep on chasing it, and why you stay in a band."

There's more to U2's longevity than that, though. Their line-up has remained unchanged since they first formed at Dublin's Mount Temple Comprehensive School 50 years ago. They remain friends first, and superstars second.

When we meet, in a bingo hall that hosted some of U2's formative gigs, there's a familial vibe to the whole operation.

They tease Mullen Jr for turning a hose on fans who climbed the wall of his parents' house in 1976; and chat animatedly about their musical obsessions ("every four-piece wants to be the Beatles," confesses Bono).

Those bonds have kept the band together through commercial and critical ups and downs, not to mention the life-altering injuries that forced Bono to cancel a 2010 US tour, and neck problems that prompted Mullen Jr to skip their 2023-2024 Las Vegas residency.

Doctors advised him to retire, but after a (risky) surgical intervention, he's back behind the kit – developing an entirely new playing style to avoid further damage.

Larry Mullen Jr says he risked paralysis by opting to have neck surgery, following years of pain behind the drum kit

His determination will be put to the test next year, when U2 embark on a massive international stadium tour, including four UK dates at London's Tottenham Hotspur Stadium next June.

The US leg will see them play some of the same venues as their friend, Ed Sheeran. So what did they make of the controversy over his recent US tour – where some venue owners pressured Sheeran into dropping his support act, Macklemore, for making pro-Palestinian comments?

"We totally support Macklemore's right as an artist to say what he wanted to say," says The Edge.

"I don't think Ed should be vilified. He was in a very difficult situation. But I commend the other young artists who decided to leave [his] tour.

"They were sticking up for an artist's right to free speech, and I think that's the issue above anything else."

He recalls several occasions where U2 themselves made risky political statements on stage.

In 1987, after Arizona's governor banned Martin Luther King Day, Bono faced death threats if he dared to play Pride (In The Name of Love) - which addresses King's assassination - in the state.

He went ahead and did it anyway, closing his eyes in anticipation of a gunshot.

"I looked up at the end of the verse and I clearly wasn't dead," he later told Mojo magazine. 'But not only that... Adam Clayton was standing in front of me."

Bono on stage with one of the "mothers of the disappeared" during 1998's Popmart world tour in Santiago, Chile

Similarly, in 1998, the band taunted Chilean dictator Augusto Pinochet during a televised concert in Santiago. At the end of the night, they invited the mothers of the victims of Pinochet's 1973 coup d'état on to the stage, who took it in turns to say the names of their children into the microphone.

"It would have been way smarter and better for us to shut up," says the Edge. "But it was artistically necessary, and we just said, 'We can't not do this'."

Reflecting further on the Macklemore controversy, he adds: "We might disagree with some of the members of the pro-Palestine movement, but we absolutely agree with the fundamentals. We absolutely agree that what's going on [in Gaza] is unconscionable and that a child's life is equally valuable, no matter what their background."

The Israeli military launched a campaign in Gaza in response to an unprecedented Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 were taken hostage.

During Israel's military campaign in Gaza more than 73,780 people have been killed, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.

Mullen Jr is equally forthright about the freedom to speak out.

"We, as a band, will fight for the right to speak your mind, as long as it doesn't incite violence," he says.

"Even if we disagree with it or don't like it, nobody - no billionaire, no promoter, no owner - has the right to censor anybody.

"And they will definitely not be censoring us, ever."

Like I said: U2 are at their best when they trust their instincts.

You've eaten dinner, you're comfortably full, and yet half an hour later you're raiding the kitchen cupboards. Sound familiar?

Research suggests about a third of people , external are snacking every night after their evening meal - for those aged 18-24, four in five are unable to resist.

Dietitian Dr Kristine Beaulieu says this spells trouble. She points to evidence showing that the more people eat , external within two hours of going to bed, the "greater the odds" of weight gain and obesity.

So, why are evening cravings so common? And what can you do to keep them in check?

Despite the fact we spend longer going without food when we are sleeping, research suggests our appetite naturally peaks in the evening, almost regardless of how much we have eaten earlier in the day.

Prof James Betts, who researches how the body handles food and energy at the University of Bath, says a big factor is that our "hunger hormone" ghrelin is generally higher later in the day.

"While it tends to be suppressed by meals, that really only happens after the first meal of the day, not after lunch or dinner."

But what you eat also matters. Meals rich in protein, fibre and volume tend to keep us satisfied for longer.

Betts says not having a nutritious or satiating evening meal can lead to a "crash" later, which sees people snack.

For others, the fear of waking up hungry during the night is also a motivating factor, while habit plays a role too.

"If snacking often happens in the same setting, the surrounding cues can start to trigger cravings," says Prof Suzanne Higgs, an expert in appetite at the University of Birmingham.

"For example, if someone usually snacks while watching TV, simply turning the TV on may make them feel like eating."

It's not just feelings of hunger that increase later in the day. Research suggests our appetite for calorie-dense foods also becomes stronger, driven by the brain's reward system rather than a genuine need for energy.

"Our liking and wanting for high-fat foods are greater later in the day compared to low-fat foods," says Beaulieu, who splits her time between the University of Leeds and University of Moncton in Canada.

"That hedonic drive can override signals of fullness, making us want to snack or eat a dessert even though we're full."

Even after a substantial evening meal, foods rich in sugar, fat or salt can continue to activate reward pathways in the brain, helping explain why many people find themselves reaching for something more.

So when you find yourself standing in front of the biscuit tin at 9pm, it may not be a lack of willpower. Your biology is stacked against you.

The evidence is mixed. But certainly eating a large meal late affects digestion and the body's normal preparation for sleep.

What about snacking? Here the research becomes less clear.

There is some evidence that foods high in refined carbohydrates and added sugars, from white bread and white rice to biscuits and cakes, may be linked to poorer sleep.

Researchers think this could be because such foods cause bigger swings in blood sugar levels and may alter some of the hormonal signals involved in regulating sleep and appetite.

However, teasing out cause and effect is difficult. People with poor sleep may be more likely to snack on sugary foods.

"Sleep deprivation is known to not only increase appetite, but also a desire for energy-dense foods," says Prof Jonathan Johnston, a sleep and body clock expert at the University of Surrey.

It means it is very difficult to draw firm conclusions on whether snacking in late evening disrupts sleep, says Betts.

"The evidence is far from clear and perhaps may reflect that some people respond differently to others to different foods before bed."

First, work out what's driving the snacking.

If you are genuinely hungry, it may help to make earlier meals more filling

If snacking is mainly habitual, changing routines and planning snacks in advance can help

"Eating while distracted, for instance watching TV, can lead people to consume more because they pay less attention to how much they've eaten," says Higgs.

But there's no need to ban evening snacks completely, says Beaulieu.

A reasonable portion of something enjoyable is often more sustainable

Keep healthy options, such as fruit, yoghurt and nuts available

Even a little chocolate every now and then is not the end of the world

"It's OK to eat those craved foods once in a while in moderation."

The trick, she says, is to make the healthy choice the default.

"If those craved foods aren't in the cupboard on a regular basis and a healthy option is, it means you are more likely to choose the healthier option."
