MN202611_11nbu4sw0x6.t: A crucial round of funding negotiations is underway in Kigali, with countries seeking to secure the resources needed to sustain global efforts to protect the ozone layer and curb emissions from powerful climate-warming gases. The negotiations, taking place during the 38th Meeting of the Parties to the Montreal Protocol, come as the world marks 10 years since the adoption of the Kigali Amendment, a landmark agreement aimed at reducing the use of hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs). At stake is up to $1.7 billion in funding for developing countries over the next three years, as governments negotiate the replenishment of the Multilateral Fund for the Implementation of the Montreal Protocol. The latest estimates, presented by the Technology and Economic Assessment Panel (TEAP), put funding requirements for 2027–2029 at between $1.230 billion and $1.692 billion, including support costs. ALSO READ: US ratifies Kigali Amendment to phase out climate super-pollutants The money would help developing countries meet their commitments to phase out hydrochlorofluorocarbons (HCFCs), which damage the ozone layer, and gradually reduce HFCs, powerful greenhouse gases widely used in refrigeration and air-conditioning systems. The Kigali Amendment, adopted in Rwanda's capital in October 2016, established a global framework for phasing down HFCs, which do not deplete the ozone layer but contribute significantly to global warming. Full implementation of the amendment could prevent up to 0.5°C of global warming by 2100. Funding negotiations Elizabeth Maruma Mrema, United Nations Assistant Secretary-General and Deputy Executive Director of the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP), expressed hope that the ongoing negotiations would deliver sufficient resources to support implementation of the amendment. She stressed the importance of ensuring cost-effective interventions while promoting sustainable cooling technologies. Replenishment of the Multilateral Fund is a key expected outcome of the meeting, alongside decisions on technical, organisational and compliance matters. However, the negotiations come amid concerns that financial pressures at both national and multilateral levels could complicate efforts to agree on a substantial funding package. ALSO READ: REMA urges switch to climate-friendly fridges The latest estimates reflect the resources required to help developing countries comply with phase-out and phase-down schedules, strengthen regulatory systems and adopt environmentally friendly cooling technologies. Other priorities include training refrigeration and air-conditioning technicians, supporting countries that consume relatively small quantities of controlled substances and introducing digital tools to improve refrigerant management. The negotiations also come at a time of increasing demand for sustainable cooling, energy-efficient refrigeration and cold-chain infrastructure, particularly in developing countries. Beyond the immediate funding cycle, estimated requirements stand at between $1.1 billion and $1.3 billion for 2030–2032, declining to between $600 million and $700 million for 2033–2035. Progress under the Kigali Amendment Mrema said the Multilateral Fund had already approved at least 91 Stage I Kigali HFC implementation plans, helping countries establish the systems and capacity needed to fulfil their commitments. These investments are already contributing to avoiding more than 78 million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent in emissions, and the work goes on, she said. She noted that the Fund had also invested millions of dollars in activities designed to strengthen national reporting systems, regulatory frameworks and institutional capacity. ALSO READ: Environmentalists buoyant as the Kigali Amendment enters into force In addition, the Fund is supporting 127 developing countries to improve the collection, transportation and environmentally sound management of used and unwanted controlled substances. According to Mrema, these interventions are helping countries adopt more sustainable approaches to refrigerant management. The broader transition is also creating opportunities to improve food security, reduce post-harvest losses and expand access to reliable cooling technologies. Anita Gikundiro, Director of Operations at ACES, emphasised the importance of equipping technicians with the skills to recover refrigerants rather than release them into the atmosphere. She also highlighted the role of training institutions in preparing professionals to handle alternative refrigerants safely. Madi Sakandé, President of the Union of Associations of Refrigeration and Air Conditioning (U3ARC), said improved refrigeration systems could help farmers preserve produce, access wider markets and reduce dependence on imported food. Citing figures attributed to the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, he said post-harvest losses in Africa remain a major challenge. ALSO READ: Climate philanthropies pledge $100m in support of Kigali Amendment He urged governments to invest in cold-storage facilities near farming communities, promote solar-powered cooling in areas with unreliable electricity and strengthen technical education. Rwanda pushes for predictable funding Rwanda has called for an ambitious and predictable replenishment of the Multilateral Fund, arguing that adequate financing is essential to translating international climate commitments into practical results. Environment Minister Bernadette Arakwiye said the transition to climate-friendly refrigerants must be supported by effective regulatory systems, technical training and clear market requirements. She noted that manufacturers had largely completed their transition but stressed that progress must be reinforced through concrete measures. Licensing, quotas, standards and technician training are what turn a treaty commitment into change in the market, and that is where our attention must stay, she said. Arakwiye emphasised that securing adequate funding should remain a priority for countries negotiating the next replenishment cycle. We start with resources, because everything else depends on them. An adequate and predictable replenishment of the Multilateral Fund is the foundation of our vision, and I ask you to support an ambitious replenishment for 2027 to 2029, she said. With that in place, we can reaffirm what we already know: that our goals are aligned with, and complementary to, the wider global commitment to sustainable development. Ozone protection, climate, energy and development are not competing agendas. Rwanda's phase-down targets Rwanda aims to reduce HFC consumption by 80 per cent by 2045 under its implementation of the Kigali Amendment. The country targets a 10 per cent reduction by 2029, followed by 30 per cent by 2035, 50 per cent by 2040 and 80 per cent by 2045. Rwanda phased out chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) in 2010 and has been implementing its Hydrochlorofluorocarbon Phase-out Management Plan since 2013. Under that programme, HCFC reduction targets were set at 10 per cent in 2015, 35 per cent in 2020 and 67.5 per cent in 2025, with complete phase-out targeted for 2030. Rwanda has also called for the endorsement of the Kigali+10 Declaration, a non-binding commitment reaffirming countries' determination to strengthen global atmospheric protection. The declaration seeks to reinforce implementation of the Kigali Amendment through greater compliance, international cooperation and sustained political commitment. A decade after the amendment's adoption, the negotiations in Kigali are expected to test countries' willingness to match their environmental commitments with the financial resources needed to deliver them.

MN202611_1jlsmiavnio.t: Six points out of six. Rwanda top Group K. A double-header against their second-placed rivals, Mali. The challenge to stay top gets harder. Resurgent Amavubi can dare to dream. Rightly so. Why not? For the first time in a long while, or even ever, Rwanda will approach a meeting with Mali, one of Africa's most-recognizable footballing nations without the familiar feeling that defeat is almost inevitable. That's what winning breeds. Stephen Constantine's team heads into their crucial 2027 Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON) double-header with something that has been missing for years: genuine belief that they can compete, challenge and perhaps make history. Both countries have made impressive starts to their qualifying campaigns, winning their opening two matches and collecting six points apiece. Rwanda defeated Liberia 3-1 in Kigali before producing an encouraging 2-1 away victory against Cape Verde in Praia, while Mali beat Cape Verde 3-1 and narrowly overcame Liberia 1-0. The similarities in their starts make the upcoming encounters particularly intriguing. For Amavubi, these two fixtures could be the defining moment: to show is indeed Rwanda is ready ripe for a seat at the high table of African football. Amavubi travel to Bamako on November 13 before hosting Mali at Amahoro Stadium four days later. With both sides level at the summit of Group K, the two matches could prove decisive in shaping the qualification race. On paper, Mali remain favourites. Their superior historical pedigree, greater depth and experience at major international tournaments make them a formidable opponent. The historical head-to-head record also favours the West Africans, who have won three of the four previous official meetings, with the other ending in a draw. Rwanda have never beaten Mali. Could this be that moment? Who knows! But experience shows that football is not always decided by history, reputations or statistics. At times, it is determined by momentum, organisation, confidence and the belief instilled in a team by its coach. These are precisely the ingredients Constantine, 64, appears to be bringing back to the Amavubi. Ever so long may it continue, for, Amavubi fans have seen many false dawns down the years. Since returning to the Rwanda hot seat in March this year, the Englishman has gradually given the team a clearer identity and renewed purpose. His influence is becoming increasingly visible, not simply through results but through the manner in which the Amavubi approach their matches. The wins against Liberia and Cape Verde were significant for different reasons. The former demonstrated Rwanda's attacking potential, while the latter was particularly encouraging because it came away from home against an opponent with a respectable international pedigree. More importantly, the players appear to be developing greater tactical awareness. Amavubi are showing improved discipline, better understanding of their responsibilities and a willingness to execute a collective game plan rather than relying solely on individual brilliance. There is also a noticeable improvement in confidence. Players, who previously appeared hesitant are beginning to express themselves, take responsibility and believe they can compete against stronger opposition. Winning has a way of transforming a dressing room, and Constantine seems to understand that psychological dimension of football as much as its technical and tactical demands. His challenge against Mali will be to translate that progress into two disciplined performances against a side capable of punishing the smallest defensive mistake, the way big teams do. For Constantine, the squad that he has summoned for the decisive double-header, offers encouraging options. The recall of defender Thierry Manzi should provide additional defensive experience, while midfielder Jean Bosco Ruboneka's return strengthens the coach'sselection possibilities. The presence of established performers such as Fiacre Ntwari, Ange Mutsinzi, Djihad Bizimana and Innocent Nshuti provides a foundation around which the coach can build his strategy. Bonheur Mugisha's situation will require attention. The Al Hazem midfielder is suspended for the first leg after accumulating yellow cards but will be available for the return encounter in Kigali. His absence in Bamako could influence Constantine's midfield selection, particularly against Mali's physically strong and technically gifted players. The first leg therefore demands tactical intelligence. Rwanda must resist the temptation to approach the match with excessive ambition. Yes, in football, sometimes they say attack is the best form of defence, but against sides like Mali you need to keep your descipline and shape. Staying compact, controlling the spaces between the defensive and midfield lines and exploiting opportunities on the counterattack could be crucial. But again, Constantine knows better. A draw in Bamako would be a valuable result, although Rwanda should not travel with a mentality of simply limiting the damage. The return match in Kigali will present another opportunity, particularly with home support behind the team. Amavubi's ambitions must nevertheless remain grounded. Rwanda’s only previous AFCON appearance came in 2004, when they finished third in their group after beating DR Congo, drawing with Guinea and losing to hosts Tunisia. More than two decades later, the country is desperate to return to Africa's biggest football stage. After two qualifiers, and six points in the bag, Amavubi has never been in a healthier spot. However, for Constantine, the objective should not merely be to improve performances but to help create a team capable of competing consistently at the highest continental level. His work has already generated optimism, but the Mali challenge represents a considerably bigger examination of that progress. Pass that test, and he becomes a legend in the making. Qualify and become a hero for millions of Amavubi fans. But first, an away victory would be historic and would put Rwanda in an exceptionally stronger position, although qualification would still need to be secured, mathematically. More realistically, collecting points across the two matches would represent a major statement of intent, and most importantly, a clearer picture of where the team is heading. And for once, I write this without any fear of contradiction, Rwanda are not approaching Mali solely with memories of previous defeats. They are going to Bamako with momentum, a coach who appears to understand how to get the best out of his players and a squad beginning to believe in its own capabilities. That psychological transformation could prove just as important as any tactical adjustment. The Amavubi have a mountain to climb, but Constantine has given them reason to believe that it is climbable. And in football, as Amavubi's recent victories have demonstrated, confidence can turn seemingly impossible challenges into genuine opportunities. Grab it and make history.

Callum Osmand and Camilo Duran were key as Celtic turned the game on its head

With an hour gone at Parkhead on Thursday, hope in the stands was in short supply.

Celtic were 1-0 down against Besiktas and heading towards a fourth straight defeat in this season's Europa League before ultimately turning it around for a 3-2 win .

Manager Martin O'Neill turned to his bench for a spark, bringing on Callum Osmand and Camilo Duran to replace Sebastian Tounekti and James Forrest out wide.

Osmand's first touch nestled in the bottom corner of Alexander Nubel's goal, just 43 seconds after the 20-year-old attacker came on.

All of a sudden, Celtic had a threat in behind and Besiktas looked rattled.

Then, on 77 minutes, O'Neill withdrew Kasper Hogh after another underwhelming display from the club record signing and moved Duran through the middle.

Osmand played Duran through with a delightful pass and the Colombian rounded Nubel before slotting Celtic into the lead.

Orkun Kokcu levelled for Besiktas with a fine strike, but Duran had the final say two minutes later, controlling Kieran Tierney's scuffed shot and beating Nubel from close range to send the home support into ecstasy.

Late Duran double downs Besiktas to give Celtic first Europa League win

Latest Celtic news, analysis and fan views

"Everything changed with the subs; Osmand coming on and Duran going through the middle," former Celtic midfielder Stiliyan Petrov said on TNT Sports. "They freed up space for Nygren and Baur. It was a really positive 30 minutes."

Not since Johannes Edvaldsson against Jeunesse d'Esch in the European Cup in September 1977 had a Celtic substitute scored twice in Europe (excluding qualifiers).

"Osmand came on, first touch put the ball in the net and that's really difficult, he can definitely score a goal. Duran has been fabulous for us all season no matter where he plays," O'Neill said of his goalscorers.

The Northern Irishman was asked whether it was a case of inspired substitutions or rather evidence that he should have started his best players.

"I'm not standing up for myself, not at all," he said.

"It was in design to do exactly what it did. We've played nine games in 25 days, some players needed a breather and you can get re-energised from coming on the field.

"I'm going to say that that was our plan and those players were going to come on the pitch at some point in the game."

'Celtic character shone through big time' - O'Neill

The contrast between Celtic's attacking play with Hogh leading the line and with Duran through the middle was stark.

The £11m Dane's effort cannot be questioned. He continued to battle to try to make things happen, but since arriving from Bodo/Glimt in the summer, he has now failed to score in 16 of his 17 Celtic appearances.

In 77 minutes against Besiktas, he didn't have a single shot and managed just one touch in the opposition box.

Duran, meanwhile, played just half an hour and scored two goals, had two shots, and registered four touches in the Besiktas box.

O'Neill has previously said he is unsure of his best team, but it is now obvious that Duran is Celtic's best option through the middle.

Despite Hogh's price tag, it feels inevitable he will be among the Celtic substitutes for high-stakes games.

"It'll be tough for Hogh," Hearts defender Craig Halkett said on TNT Sports. "He was the big-money singing but it's not coming off for him.

"As a player you need to keep your head down, keep working hard and hope it turns."

Osmand too appears to have pushed himself to the front of the queue to start off the left. The former Fulham man is direct and evidently has an eye for goal, with a happy knack for scoring in big games.

"This is a great team we're playing against," Osmand told TNT Sports. "Camilo [Duran] did amazing, he's such a poacher. Credit to him.

"It's a lot harder starting games. The team dug in, stayed strong and we got our rewards.

"[The goal] caught me off guard, but I'm just glad I caught it nice. I just want to come on and make something happen. So happy with tonight."

A jet engine will have hundreds of turbine blades

Every time you fly, an extraordinary feat of endurance occurs inside the aircraft's engines.

Hidden from view inside the sleek outer nacelle are hundreds of little turbine blades that can shrug off enormous mechanical stresses and temperatures exceeding 1,500C.

It is a true engineering marvel. And these hardy blades are not sculpted or cut from their material – they are grown.

During the 1960s, engineers worked out how to take a molten metal alloy, cast it into the shape of a turbine blade, and then cool it very carefully from one end to the other over a matter of hours. A single crystal or grain of metal alloy forms during this process of gradual, delicate solidification.

Like turning a cup of water into one big snowflake, of your own design, rather than a mini blizzard of many smaller snowflakes.

"It's about as complicated as manufacturing gets," says Ben Fifoot, manufacturing engineer at Rolls-Royce, which makes turbine blades in the UK. "It's a real motivator to get out of bed in the morning."

Only a handful of companies around the world can produce these single crystal turbine blades, and the process has been perfected end-to-end in just five countries, including the US and UK. Engine-makers continually vie for access to the technology.

Rolls-Royce, GE and France's Safran are among the few firms that have perfected the process.

In September, GE Aerospace announced , external it would acquire its turbine blade supplier for $11.75bn (£8.78bn). Neither company responded to BBC News' requests for comment but the move has been described as an effort to ensure supply of these critical components.

Separately, in March, Rolls-Royce said it would invest more than £19m in its Rotherham blade casting facility.

Turbine blade specialists continue to work on improving the capabilities of this little-known technology. All the while, China is desperate to prove that its engineers can produce turbine blades of the same quality as those in the West. Who will come out on top?

"Demand for [turbine blades] is huge. So few companies have managed to do it, which does give it this kind of magical aura," says Bill Sweetman, an aviation industry writer and consultant.

He suspects GE Aerospace's recent move is about securing reliability and predictability in the notoriously volatile aircraft manufacturing supply chain.

The casts play a crucial part in the cooling process

But why is the single crystal casting process, which has been around for decades now, still so specialist?

To grow one of these blades, asserts Fifoot, is to "fight the laws of the universe".

This is because each molten blade would naturally cool into a solid object consisting of many small grains of metal alloy, all jumbled together. But you don't want a crumbly sugar cube, you want a perfect diamond.

Getting a single crystal to grow into the shape of the blade instead isn't just a matter of cooling the molten version down slowly, the process also uses a bizarre trick called a pigtail.

The pigtail is a small spiral at one end of the blade. Fifoot says that, at the beginning of the cooling process, this spiral "chokes" the flow of solidifying crystals so that just one takes over. A bit like a hairpin corner in an F1 race right before the finish line – one driver can take the lead here and go on to win.

"Sometimes we need to play around with the number of turns or the angles on [the pigtail] to try and get more favourable grain," adds Fifoot. Once the blade is formed, this crucial but sacrificial spiral is cut off.

France's Safran is among the few companies that can make single crystal blades

Blades made by Rolls-Royce are used in aircraft engines including the Trent XWB-84, which powers the Airbus A350-900, and the Trent 1000 XE, for the Boeing 787.

The single crystal is essential to ensure each blade's performance. Sometimes a blade doesn't cool quite as planned, for example two crystals form within it instead of just one, and the metal alloy must be reprocessed so that the manufacturer may re-use the material.

Special ceramic coatings also protect blades from extreme temperatures inside engines. And another important feature is that blades are cast with tiny channels that allow a flow of cooler air to coat them in a kind of film while the aircraft engine is working.

"The drive at the moment [across the industry] is currently to make those cooling passages really intricate," says Paul Withey, at the University of Birmingham, who formerly worked for Rolls-Royce. The more turbulent those little flows of cool air are, he explains, the more they will knock heat out of the surrounding, much hotter air.

And blade-makers also seek to reduce the mass of these components as much as possible.

"If we can take any weight out of it, you can run that engine more efficiently using less fuel – you can spin it faster and hotter," says Fifoot.

The turbine blades are used in the Trent 1000 engine among others

Meanwhile, China hopes to become only the sixth country to master the whole technology chain for single crystal blade casting.

A report in May , external quoted one engineer at the AECC Beijing Institute of Aeronautical Materials claiming that China now had a single crystal alloy "superior to or equivalent to the second-generation single-crystal superalloys widely used in Europe and the US". It costs less to make, too, apparently.

But the West has a "huge advantage" over China given that the majority of commercial airliner production happens there, says Sweetman. Supply chains and the latest innovations are generally clustered in the West. Plus, Western manufacturers also have lengthy safety records under their belts.

China must compete on practically every aspect of aircraft manufacturing , external – by no means just on turbine blades – in order to make serious in-roads. "You can definitely see that happening but it's a long, uphill struggle," adds Sweetman.

Demand for aircraft is currently high, which is already straining various supply chains in the industry. That demand could grow higher still, suggests Withey.

During the next few years, one of the two main aircraft manufacturers, Airbus and Boeing, could launch a new short-haul plane , external , he says. Then, the other would have to follow suit in order to remain competitive.

"There'll be a bun fight," says Withey, over who gets to supply the engines and, by extension, those all-important single crystal turbine blades.

Pope Leo is travelling to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru

Pope Leo XIV is beginning a lengthy trip to Latin America just three weeks after surgery for lung cancer - a tour that includes a much-anticipated "homecoming" to Peru where he was a priest for many years.

The Vatican says no extraordinary measures are being taken in relation to the Pope's health, describing him as a "71-year-old who has undergone an operation" not someone with a "permanent medical condition".

It was Leo himself who revealed last month that doctors had discovered a tumour during a routine scan. The growth was removed along with the lower lobe of his right lung and his medical team then confirmed the cancer had not spread.

At a briefing in Rome ahead of the trip, which takes in Uruguay and Argentina as well as Peru, a spokeswoman stressed that Pope Leo had "fantastic stamina" and was "extremely enthusiastic" about the schedule which he had "personally confirmed... with no changes".

"The Vatican's message with this trip is, 'that was a short episode and now we're back on track'," Professor Massimo Faggioli of Villanova University told the BBC, pointing out that the Pope has had a busy return to work since his surgery.

"We have seen him in these last few days making speeches, audiences and so on. He seems in great shape. That was important."

On Friday Pope Leo presided over the annual memorial Mass for cardinals and bishops who have died

The 12-day tour would be demanding for anyone, though. It incorporates multiple long-haul and local flights and covers thousands of miles from the Amazon to the Andes.

The starting point will be Uruguay, where the number of Catholics has fallen away steeply in recent years and which is getting its first Papal visit in four decades.

Leo then heads for Argentina, homeland of Pope Francis, his predecessor.

Father Fernando Laguna said his heart was filled with joy when the Pope's visit to Argentina was announced

"This visit is also a homage to Francis, who didn't make it to Argentina [as pope]," says Father Fernando Laguna, the rector of Santa Maria Addolorata, Argentina's national church in Rome.

"When this visit by Pope Leo was announced, it filled all of our hearts with joy," he told the BBC. "I always thought he would go, despite his illness. I don't think he ever thought of calling it off!"

The priest is installing a big screen inside the church in Rome to allow parishioners to follow all the key moments of the trip from afar. The building is already decked out with posters declaring Pope Leo is welcome in Argentina. "We're waiting for you!", one proclaims.

'Welcome Pope Leo' reads this poster in the Argentinian church in Rome

This leg of the Pope's journey - which includes meetings with heads of state as well as religious events - could be the most politically sensitive. President Javier Milei once called Pope Francis "evil on earth" and a "communist" for promoting a doctrine of social justice to help the poor. In turn, Argentina's bishops have criticised Milei's harsh austerity measures, making sweeping cuts to social spending.

But Milei has already welcomed Pope Leo, writing in a post on X that Argentina awaits "with immense joy". Millions are expected to turn out to greet him.

The highlight of the trip is undoubtedly saved for last, when Pope Leo reaches Peru - described by the Vatican as a return to his roots.

"He knows these streets," is how a spokeswoman put it.

Worshippers at Chiclayo cathedral in Peru were delighted when their former bishop became Pope in 2025

Born in the US, the then Robert Prevost spent almost 20 years in Peru, on and off, and even has Peruvian citizenship. That time is seen as fundamental to shaping his papacy.

His schedule includes a return to the diocese of Chiclayo where he was ordained bishop in 2014 and remained until Francis moved him to the Vatican almost a decade later.

He will also travel to Cusco, former capital of the Inca Empire, to say Mass more than 3,000m above sea level before heading to Pucallpa in the Amazon.

In all three countries, the Vatican says the Pope will have meetings with survivors of clerical sexual abuse - an issue which clouded a 2018 visit to Chile and Peru by his predecessor.

"This is how the papacy reconnects with Latin America after Francis, whose visits to the region were not always seamless," is how Professor Faggioli sees it.

He believes Pope Leo has a strong sense of the unity of the Americas as one continent. "Democracies are in trouble there, so there are so many things he can address," he suggests.

"The big question then is the United States. There's no question he wants to go. So will he travel when [President Donald] Trump is still in office? I'm sure they're thinking about this."

Watch: What was your worst ever job interview?

Tiara Allen arrived on time to interview for a retail job. Her interviewer didn't.

She waited for around 40 minutes in a shopping centre while the interviewer's co-worker called them "two or three times".

When they finally showed up, Tiara says she was told it was because the meeting wasn't in the schedule.

She needed work at the time, so took the job when she was offered it, but says she would handle the situation differently now.

"I would not take a job if they took that long," she says, adding that she believed her treatment during the interview was a sign of how the firm tended to treat staff.

Tiara Allen says she took the job despite being made to wait 40 minutes before the interview because she needed work

Tiara is far from alone. She is one of many people who spoke to the BBC about their worst job interview experiences after we wrote about the one interview question that leaves you feeling uncomfortable .

While those situations can be hard to deal with in the moment, they can also teach us a lot about the world of work.

During an interview for an assistant at a book publisher in New York, Chas Edwards was asked a question he wasn't expecting.

"I was asked for my first job if I was a crier," he recalls.

Thinking the interviewer was being funny, Chas replied that he didn't cry. He was later told that this was why he got the job.

"Her last assistant had cried – too often, I guess? – and she wanted someone who didn't cry. So she was being serious and I thought it was a joke," he says.

It was a bad sign. Chas says it was "a terrible, terrible job with a miserable boss" and while he managed to make it through 13 months there without crying he was "crying inside".

"I set the world record for working for this person. No-one had ever lasted three months with her before," he recalls.

Despite all this, Chas says he is in some ways grateful the experience was so awful.

"Because every job since then, even the bad ones, are not that bad," he says, adding that he can "cry anywhere now".

Chas Edwards says he thought the interviewer's question for his first job was a joke

Corinne Card also found herself floored when the first question she was asked in an interview for an administrative job was if she liked working with people.

When she replied yes, she was told that the job wouldn't be for her and the interview ended there.

"I don't know if it was a deliberate trap. Because who would answer 'I don't like working with people'?"

Corinne Mills, joint managing director of Personal Career Management, says that it can be worth asking an interviewer to clarify any weird questions, perhaps by repeating the question back to them.

However, if a line of questioning is really off-putting, she says it can also be a sign of what it's like to work there, saying that interviews are also about candidates judging the company.

Meanwhile, other questions are not just annoying – they are illegal.

Discrimination against a protected characteristic is against the law , external , meaning an employer cannot treat you less favourably based on your age, disability, gender reassignment, marriage, pregnancy, race, religion, sex, or sexual orientation.

Employment lawyer Roy Magara says that women being asked if they intend on having children in an interview is a "quite common" kind of bias. He says he has also seen a case where an older candidate was told he didn't get the job after an interview because he didn't fit the "vibe" of a younger team.

If you think these sorts of biases took place in your interview, Roy says you can send the company a subject access request , external to see how they discussed your application internally.

Worst-case scenarios like these can make interviews feel very difficult, especially considering the control employers have over candidates.

Euan Cameron, co-founder of hiring software Willo, says that even with this power imbalance it's important not to overthink what an interview is.

"An interview is just a conversation between two people," he says.

Of course, as in Tiara's case, it helps when both of those people show up.

Liva AI collects multimodal interaction data through consumer products used by real people. Because Liva owns both the collection environment and distribution, it can design products around specific model gaps across domains, industries, languages, modalities, and interaction types. This gives it access to natural, high-context behavior that emerges through real product use, rather than artificially elicited or task-based interactions.
